A few practical tips if you want them:
- Go to one meet-up first as a participant to get the vibe and observe what volunteers actually do.
- Ask the organizer what they most need (setup/cleanup, greeter, food coordination, workshop leader, childcare, outreach, socials).
- Pick a role that fits your time and energy — smaller, reliable tasks (e.g., welcoming people, running a sign-up sheet, making name tags) make a big difference.
- Prepare a simple icebreaker or way to introduce people so newcomers feel included (examples below).
- If you lead a skill-share, plan a short, hands-on session (20–40 minutes) with clear takeaways and materials list.
- Set boundaries: commit only to what you can manage and ask for support if something feels overwhelming.

Quick icebreaker ideas:
- “What’s one thing you learned this year?”
- Two-truths-one-skill (focuses on abilities rather than just facts)
- A quick shared task: “In groups, arrange these community needs by priority” — gets people talking and problem-solving.

If you want, tell me what skills you might share or what kind of role appeals to you and I can suggest a short workshop plan or a friendly intro message to send the organizer.

messages.speaker: responder_agent
messages.content:
Sounds like a great plan — starting as a participant and volunteering for greeting/setup/cleanup is a low-pressure way to help. A few focused tips and ready-to-use items so you feel prepared:

Quick logistics
- arrive 20–30 minutes before start (gives time to set up and meet the organizer)
- bring a small toolkit: tape, scissors, Sharpie, name tags, sticky notes, trash bags, hand sanitizer, paper towels
- wear a visible name tag and comfortable shoes

Greeter basics
- position yourself near the entrance but not blocking traffic; smile, make eye contact
- have a simple sign-in sheet or clipboard, nametags, and a printed schedule or agenda to hand out
- welcome lines (choose one that fits your tone):
  - Warm: “Hi — welcome! I’m [Name]. Is this your first time here?”  
  - Practical: “Hi — welcome back/first time! Here’s the agenda and a nametag. Can I answer any questions?”  
  - For shy folks: “Hi — I’m [Name]. I’ll be around if you want a tour of the room or to meet someone.”
- if someone’s new, introduce them to one or two people with a quick connector (“This is Alex — they’re into gardening; Alex, meet Sam who organizes the plant swaps.”)
- note accessibility needs and any childcare arrangements to relay to the organizer

Setup checklist
- seating layout (chairs/tables), extension cords, and projector/AV tested
- signage (directional signs, program schedule)
- food table & labels for allergens, napkins, utensils, plates
- a clear drop zone for coats/bags
- volunteer assignments posted (who does what and when)

Cleanup checklist
- designate a trash/recycling/compost station and empty food/condiment containers
- wipe tables, fold chairs, sweep if needed
- collect lost-and-found items and take a photo of them
- restore furniture/AV to original positions
- count remaining supplies and note what to restock
- quick post-event check-in with organizer: what went well, what to adjust

Dealing with issues
- for conflict or medical emergencies, alert the lead organizer immediately
- for overwhelmed newcomers, offer to pair them with a small group activity or introduce them to someone with similar interests

Short icebreaker (5–10 min)
- “Two-minute story”: in pairs, each person shares one thing they learned recently. Rotate once so everyone meets two people. Good for quick connections without pressure.

Sample message you can send the organizer to offer help
“Hi [Organizer name], I’m planning to attend the next meet-up and would love to help with greeting or setup/cleanup. I can arrive ~20–30 minutes early to help set up or stay after to tidy. Let me know what would be most useful. — [Your name]”

- draft a volunteer assignment sheet,
- or make a 20–30 minute skill-share outline if you decide to lead something later.

Quick greeter script (pick your tone)
- Warm: “Hi — welcome! I’m [Name]. Is this your first time here?”  
- Practical: “Welcome back/first time! Here’s the agenda and a nametag. Can I answer any questions?”  
- Low-pressure for shy folks: “I’m [Name]. If you want a quick tour or to meet someone, I’m happy to introduce you.”  
If someone’s new, offer a connector: “This is Alex — they’re into gardening; Alex, meet Sam who organizes the plant swaps.”

Sign-in & nametag basics
- Keep the clipboard/sign-in near the door; gently ask guests to sign in for updates.  
- Put nametags on the right shoulder so they’re readable during handshakes.  
- Provide a printed agenda and a map of the space if it’s large. Note allergy labels for food and a small sign asking permission before taking photos.

Running the two-minute-story icebreaker (5–10 minutes total)
- Explain (30s): “We’ll do a two-minute story. Pair up; each person has one minute to share something they learned recently. After one minute, swap.”  
- Pairing (30s): Pair neighbors quickly (count off or have people find the nearest person).  
- Timing (2–3 minutes per pair): Use a soft timer or signal to swap.  
- Inclusion tweak: If someone prefers not to speak, they can listen and then tell the group one fact about themselves.  
- Wrap-up (1–2 min): Invite 2–3 volunteers to share a highlight or invite everyone to continue chats over refreshments.

Handling common situations
- Overwhelmed newcomer: Offer to introduce them to someone with shared interests and point out quiet corners.  
- Accessibility: Ask quietly if they need any accommodations (seating, sound, mobility); flag to organizer.  
- Conflicts/medical issues: Alert the lead organizer immediately — don’t try to manage serious issues alone.

Small kit to bring
- Nametags + marker, sign-in clipboard, printed agendas, tape/scissors, hand sanitizer, spare pens, and allergy labels for food.

  - Communicate with parents about allergies/safety; keep an eye on entrances/exits
  - Supplies: toys, art supplies, wipes, small trash bag, seating

- Food Table / Allergy Monitor (1–2)
  - Arrange snacks, label allergens, maintain napkins/plates/utensils
  - Keep food area tidy and restock as needed
  - Supplies: labels, marker, trash/recycling bins, hand sanitizer

- AV / Tech Helper (1, optional)
  - Handle microphone, music, slides, or projector; troubleshoot minor tech issues
  - Supplies: cords, adapter, spare batteries

- Floaters / Connectors (1–2)
  - Circulate, introduce newcomers to others, check on people who look unsure, help with errands
  - Great role for friendly people who like mingling

- Cleanup Crew (2–3)
  - Clear food, wipe tables, fold chairs, sweep if needed, collect lost-and-found, restore space
  - Take a quick inventory of supplies to restock for next event
  - Supplies: trash bags, cleaning wipes, broom

Quick shift plan & timings
- Arrival: all volunteers 20–30 min before start (setup)
- Start: greeters at door; Lead Organizer does welcome/checklist
- Mid-event: floaters support activities and newcomers
- End: cleanup crew begins as program winds down; volunteers stay ~20–30 min after

End-of-event checklist
- Collect sign-in sheet and contact info for organizer
- Box up leftover food (label & store or discard per organizer)
- Wipe tables, fold chairs, return equipment, sweep floor
- Photo/log of lost-and-found; post or message organizer for pickup
- Quick 5-min debrief with organizer: what went well, what to change

Safety & troubleshooting
- Medical emergency: call 911 immediately and notify Lead Organizer
- Lost child: calm search, announce to volunteers, check exits, contact parents
- Conflicts: de-escalate calmly, move people to a quieter area, get Lead Organizer
- Accessibility: ask quietly how we can help (seating, hearing, mobility)

Notes & tips
- Wear comfortable shoes and a visible volunteer name tag
- Keep interactions warm but brief at the door to avoid bottlenecks
- Encourage people to sign in only once per household; respect privacy

Goal statement
- Deliver a compliant, production-ready Payments API v2 in 9 weeks while preserving stability for current customers, aligning stakeholders, and putting repeatable delivery practices in place.

High-level timeline & key decision points
- Week 0–2 (by end of 2nd week): Scope/Decision freeze (what must ship for compliance vs. nice-to-have).
- Week 5–6: Feature freeze (no new features; only bug/ compliance fixes).
- Week 7: User acceptance, security & compliance sign-offs completed.
- Week 8–9: Production rollout (canary -> full), monitoring & rollback plan active.
- Post-launch Weeks 10–13: Stabilize, retro, and roadmap for next quarter.

First 30 days — Assess, align, and lock scope (listen + plan fast)
Primary objective
- Clarify compliance requirements, lock minimal viable scope for v2, align stakeholders, and get the team focused on a single prioritized plan.

Key actions
- Rapid stakeholder alignment workshops (60–90 min): Legal/Compliance, Product, Sales, Finance, Security. Produce a single one-page requirements & acceptance criteria doc for compliance items and non-compliance scope tradeoffs.
- Run 1:1s with all 8 team members to surface risks, capacity, and blockers (30–45 min each).
- Technical audit: engineering to produce current status of API spec, compatibility impacts, migration plan, open technical debt that blocks compliance.
- QA & security plan: QA owner to draft test matrix (functional, regression, performance) and Security to list required audits/pen tests and timelines.
- Create release schedule & decision timeline with explicit cutoffs (scope freeze, feature freeze, code freeze).
- Define RACI for every compliance deliverable (who signs off, who implements, escalation path).
- Quick wins: fix 1–2 highest-impact, low-effort blockers (e.g., automated test failing pipelines, flaky integration tests, missing monitoring).

Success metrics (end of day 30)
- Signed scope & decision freeze doc with stakeholders.
- Release schedule with cutoffs published and shared.
- Completed 1:1s and a short team health pulse.
- Threat list & top 10 risks documented with mitigation owners.
- CI pipeline stable and a reproducible staging environment.

Days 31–60 — Execute, validate, and lock (deliver & QA)
Primary objective
- Execute the committed scope, validate compliance requirements, stabilize builds, and get to a releasable state.

Key actions
- Split remaining work into 2-week delivery sprints with clear sprint goals aligned to compliance milestones.
- Implement required API changes, versioning/migration strategy, and docs for integrators.
- QA ramp-up: full regression suite runs in CI; end-to-end tests against staging; test data prepared for compliance scenarios.
- Security & compliance tests: run pen-tests, privacy checks, and produce audit artifacts. Work with Legal to address findings on the same sprint cadence.
- Performance testing: identify throughput/latency targets; run load tests that mirror production traffic.
- Integration partners: coordinate with any external integrators (Sales/Finance customers) for early validation and compatibility tests.
- Communication: weekly stakeholder sync (30–45 min) with a short status one-pager, risks, and decisions needed. Daily stand-ups with engineered blockers escalated to you.
- Resource contingency: if QA capacity is a bottleneck, request temporary contractor or shift designer resources to support integration test automation.

Milestones & freeze timelines (suggested)
- End of Week 6: Feature freeze — only compliance/critical bug fixes allowed.
- End of Week 7: Complete compliance signoffs and security remediation.
- Day ~50: Code freeze; prep release candidates.

Success metrics (end of day 60)
- Release candidate built and deployed to staging with passing regression & security checks.
- Compliance signoff completed or documented with outstanding minimal items and mitigation plans.
- Automated tests covering critical flows; flaky tests reduced to acceptable threshold.
- Stakeholders confirm readiness and rollback/communication plans exist.

Days 61–90 — Launch, monitor, and institutionalize
Primary objective
- Safely roll out v2, monitor production impact, and lock learnings into the team’s operating rhythm.

Key actions
- Controlled rollout: Canary or limited-customer rollout first; monitor health, metrics and rollback triggers (errors, latency, business KPIs).
- Full rollout: expand after canary validation window (predefined).
- Post-launch monitoring & ops: have runbooks, alerting, SLA owners, and an on-call rotation (cover first 72 hours intensely).
- Post-launch retrospective (within 2 weeks): review what worked, what didn’t, and update checklist for next release.
- Customer communication & docs: publish migration guide, changelog, and support FAQs; train Sales and Support on talking points.
- Career/capability planning: set 1:1 development goals with direct reports based on ramp insights.

Success metrics (end of day 90)
- v2 is live for targeted customers; canary and full rollout completed with no critical incidents.
- Compliance audit artifacts accepted; no open high-severity compliance findings.
- Key KPIs stable/improved: error rate within target, latency within SLA, integration failure rate minimal.
- Documented release runbook, lessons learned, and a proposed roadmap for post-v2 improvements.

Risks & mitigation (top items)
- Risk: Regulatory delay or last-minute Legal demands. Mitigation: early Legal engagement, prioritize compliance items, maintain a contingency scope that can be cut without impacting compliance.
- Risk: Scope creep from stakeholders (Sales/PM). Mitigation: decision freeze & RACI; negotiate nonessential items to later patch release.
- Risk: QA bottleneck or flaky tests. Mitigation: increase automated tests early, bring in temporary QA support, dedicate a day for flaky-test stabilization.
- Risk: Third-party vendor integration delays. Mitigation: parallelize work where possible; create fallback/feature-flag plans.

Communication cadences & artifacts
- Weekly stakeholder sync (30–45 min) + one-page status (progress, decisions required, top risks).
- Weekly internal demo for team & manager (show progress, surface impediments).
- Decision log (who decided what, when) and a single source-of-truth release timeline document.
- Daily stand-ups + a short daily escalation note for execs during final 2 weeks.

Immediate asks you can make to your manager/stakeholders (to unblock success)

- Approval for temporary QA/contractor support if needed.
- Exec alignment on rollback thresholds and customer communication templates.

3) KPI dashboard template — activation, retention, and MRR
Dashboard goal: provide one live view for launch-day monitoring (real-time signals) and a compact analysis view for post-launch decisions (daily + cohort analysis).

Top-level layout (widgets)
- Header: product name, last updated timestamp, launch status (green/amber/red), owner contact  
- North-star & top-line metrics (big numbers)
  - Activation rate (X-day): % of new users who complete the activation funnel within 7 days  
  - DAU/WAU/MAU (as relevant) or weekly active users for target segment  
  - Net New MRR (period) and Net MRR growth %  
  - Churn rate (monthly) and Expansion MRR
- Real-time launch signals (first 72 hours)
  - Live funnel: visits → signups → activation step 1 → activation completion  
  - Error/exception rate, support tickets opened labeled “launch”  
  - Feature usage heatmap (top events) and latency/availability alerts
- Cohort retention section
  - Retention curves for day 1, day 7, day 30 cohorts (by acquisition source and by plan)  
  - Rolling retention table and D7/D30 retention %
- MRR breakdown
  - New MRR, Expansion MRR, Contraction MRR, Churned MRR (period-to-period)

- Experiments & actions

- Recent issues & action log

Metric definitions & formulas (use consistent naming)
- Activation rate (7-day) = # of new users who reach activation event within 7 days of signup / # of new users (signup cohort)  
  - Define activation event precisely (e.g., completed onboarding checklist item X, created first project, connected payment, performed transaction)  
- Retention (N-day) = % of users from cohort who perform the “key action” on day N or within a retention window  
  - Report D1, D7, D30 and 7-day rolling retention. Segment by source/plan.  
- Net New MRR (period) = New MRR + Expansion MRR - Contraction MRR - Churned MRR  
  - New MRR: MRR from new subscriptions in period  
  - Expansion MRR: upgrades, add-ons in period  
  - Contraction MRR: downgrades/refunds in period  
  - Churned MRR: lost subscription MRR

Instrumentation (events & properties to ensure)
- Required events:
  - user_signed_up {user_id, time, plan, source, campaign_id}  
  - activation_step_completed {user_id, time, step_name} — define final activation event activation_completed {user_id, time}  
  - feature_used {user_id, feature_name, time, context}  
  - billing_event {user_id, time, event_type:new/upgrade/downgrade/cancel, mrr_delta}

- Required user properties:
  - created_at, plan, account_id, cohort_source, region, sales_segment
- Ensure events include account-level IDs for SaaS billing mapping

Visuals & priorities during launch
- On launch day: monitor the funnel and error rate minute-by-minute for first 3 hours, hourly for next 24 hours, and daily thereafter. Set alerts for:
  - Activation funnel drop > X% vs baseline or baseline trend (e.g., 30% drop)  
  - Error rate spike > Y (e.g., 5% of requests) or availability < 99% for the launch flow

Cadence & ownership

- Daily launch report (first 7 days): Product owner (you) — publish brief summary to execs and stake holders.  
- Weekly growth review (post-launch): Product + Marketing + CS + Sales + Analytics — review experiments and adjustments.

Implementation notes / quick-start

1) Amplitude event list & required properties (canonical names)
Notes: keep event names kebab/camel consistent (below uses snake_case). For Amplitude, send the event + these properties as event properties; also set user properties for persistent attributes.

Core events (required)
- user_signed_up
  - properties: user_id, account_id, created_at (ts), plan, plan_id, source, campaign_id, referrer, region
  - user property suggestion: signup_date

- activation_step_completed
  - properties: user_id, account_id, event_time, step_name (e.g., onboarding_tour_complete / first_project_created / payment_method_added), session_id, source

- activation_completed
  - properties: user_id, account_id, event_time, session_id, signup_date
  - define this as the canonical activation event (the final step in funnel)

- session_start
  - properties: user_id, account_id, event_time, session_id, device, platform

- feature_used
  - properties: user_id, account_id, event_time, feature_name, context (page/flow), session_id

- subscription_created (or billing_subscribed)
  - properties: user_id, account_id, event_time, plan, plan_id, mrr_delta (numeric), currency, subscription_id, source

- subscription_updated
  - properties: user_id, account_id, event_time, plan_previous, plan_new, mrr_delta, subscription_id, reason (if known)

- subscription_canceled
  - properties: user_id, account_id, event_time, subscription_id, mrr_delta (negative), cancel_reason, cancel_initiator (user/CS/sales)

- billing_event (generic)
  - properties: user_id, account_id, event_time, event_type (new/upgrade/downgrade/cancel/refund), mrr_delta, amount, currency, invoice_id

- support_ticket_opened
  - properties: user_id, account_id, event_time, ticket_id, channel (email/chat/phone), severity (P0/P1/etc), topic, launch_tag (boolean)

- support_ticket_closed
  - properties: ticket_id, account_id, user_id, event_time, time_to_resolution_seconds, severity, topic

- error_occurred
  - properties: user_id (nullable), account_id (nullable), event_time, error_code, error_message, endpoint, stack_trace_id, severity

Optional / experiments
- experiment_viewed / experiment_exposure
  - properties: experiment_id, variant, user_id, account_id, event_time, metric_targeted

Required user / account properties (user properties / device properties)

- account: account_id, plan, mrr (current), billing_plan_start, sales_segment, industry, account_owner_id

Instrumentation notes

- Ensure timestamps are in ISO / UTC and that event properties are typed correctly (numerics for mrr_delta).
- Tag support tickets and errors that are related to the launch with launch_tag=true.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
2) Day‑0 dashboard mock — layout + SQL snippets for each tile
Assumptions for SQL snippets
- Warehouse: BigQuery (standard SQL).  
- Primary event table: `events` with columns:
  - event_name STRING
  - user_id STRING
  - account_id STRING
  - event_time TIMESTAMP
  - event_date DATE
  - step_name STRING
  - feature_name STRING
  - plan STRING
  - source STRING
  - mrr_delta NUMERIC
  - error_code STRING
  - severity STRING
  - ticket_id STRING
  - properties JSON/STRING (if needed)
- Users table: `users` (user_id, created_at, account_id, plan, region)
- Accounts table: `accounts` (account_id, current_mrr, sales_segment)

Replace names with your real tables/columns.

Top header (single-row)
- Launch status (green/amber/red) — manual or driven by presence of critical P0s
- Last updated timestamp
- Owner: [your name] (static)

Top-line KPIs (big numbers, single value tiles)
1) Activation rate (7-day) — for signups in rolling 7-day window
SQL (activation rate = % of users who completed activation within 7 days of signup):

WITH signups AS (
  SELECT user_id, DATE(created_at) AS signup_date
  FROM users
  WHERE DATE(created_at) BETWEEN DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 7 DAY) AND CURRENT_DATE()
)
, activated AS (
  SELECT s.user_id
  FROM signups s
  JOIN events e
    ON e.user_id = s.user_id
    AND e.event_name = 'activation_completed'
    AND DATE(e.event_time) BETWEEN s.signup_date AND DATE_ADD(s.signup_date, INTERVAL 7 DAY)
  GROUP BY s.user_id
)
SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM activated) AS activated_users,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM signups) AS signups,
  SAFE_DIVIDE((SELECT COUNT(*) FROM activated), (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM signups)) AS activation_rate_7d

2) DAU (or WAU)
SQL (DAU today):

SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS dau
FROM events
WHERE DATE(event_time) = CURRENT_DATE()
  AND event_name IN ('session_start','feature_used','activation_completed')

3) Net New MRR (last 30 days)
SQL:

WITH billing AS (
  SELECT
    DATE(event_time) AS day,
    SUM(COALESCE(mrr_delta,0)) AS mrr_delta
  FROM events
  WHERE event_name IN ('subscription_created','subscription_updated','subscription_canceled','billing_event')
    AND DATE(event_time) BETWEEN DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 30 DAY) AND CURRENT_DATE()
  GROUP BY day
)
SELECT
  SUM(mrr_delta) AS net_new_mrr_30d
FROM billing

4) D7 retention (for signup cohort 7 days ago — or rolling cohorts)
SQL (example for cohorts by signup_date last 14 days; returns D1/D7/D30 retention):

WITH cohort AS (
  SELECT user_id, DATE(created_at) AS signup_date FROM users
  WHERE DATE(created_at) BETWEEN DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 30 DAY) AND CURRENT_DATE()
)
, actions AS (
  SELECT user_id, DATE(event_time) AS action_date
  FROM events
  WHERE event_name = 'feature_used' -- define "key action" or use activation_completed
)
SELECT
  c.signup_date,
  COUNT(DISTINCT c.user_id) AS cohort_size,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN DATE_DIFF(a.action_date, c.signup_date, DAY) = 1 THEN a.user_id END) AS d1_active,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN DATE_DIFF(a.action_date, c.signup_date, DAY) = 7 THEN a.user_id END) AS d7_active,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN DATE_DIFF(a.action_date, c.signup_date, DAY) = 30 THEN a.user_id END) AS d30_active
FROM cohort c
LEFT JOIN actions a ON a.user_id = c.user_id
GROUP BY c.signup_date
ORDER BY c.signup_date DESC

Funnel widget (minute/hourly on Day‑0 for: visits → signups → activation step → activation_completed)
SQL (hourly funnel counts last 24 hours):

WITH events_filtered AS (
  SELECT event_name, DATE_TRUNC(event_time, HOUR) AS hour_bucket
  FROM events
  WHERE event_time BETWEEN TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 24 HOUR) AND CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()
    AND event_name IN ('page_view','user_signed_up','activation_step_completed','activation_completed')
)
SELECT
  hour_bucket,
  SUM(CASE WHEN event_name = 'page_view' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS page_views,
  SUM(CASE WHEN event_name = 'user_signed_up' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS signups,
  SUM(CASE WHEN event_name = 'activation_step_completed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS activation_steps,
  SUM(CASE WHEN event_name = 'activation_completed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS activation_completed
FROM events_filtered
GROUP BY hour_bucket
ORDER BY hour_bucket

Cohort heatmap (D0–D30 retention) — reuse the cohort query but pivot / render as heatmap in Looker

MRR waterfall (tile + stacked bars)
SQL (30d breakdown: new, expansion, contraction, churn):

WITH billing_events AS (
  SELECT
    DATE(event_time) AS day,
    CASE
      WHEN event_name = 'subscription_created' THEN 'new'
      WHEN event_name = 'subscription_updated' AND mrr_delta > 0 THEN 'expansion'
      WHEN event_name = 'subscription_updated' AND mrr_delta < 0 THEN 'contraction'
      WHEN event_name = 'subscription_canceled' THEN 'churn'
      ELSE 'other'
    END AS bucket,
    SUM(COALESCE(mrr_delta,0)) AS mrr_sum
  FROM events
  WHERE event_name IN ('subscription_created','subscription_updated','subscription_canceled','billing_event')
    AND DATE(event_time) BETWEEN DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 30 DAY) AND CURRENT_DATE()
  GROUP BY day, bucket
)
SELECT bucket, SUM(mrr_sum) AS mrr_value
FROM billing_events
GROUP BY bucket
ORDER BY FIELD(bucket,'new','expansion','contraction','churn')

Support tickets & P0/P1 triage table
SQL (tickets in last 72 hours with time to resolution):

SELECT
  ticket_id,
  account_id,
  severity,
  topic,
  MIN(CASE WHEN event_name = 'support_ticket_opened' THEN event_time END) AS opened_at,
  MIN(CASE WHEN event_name = 'support_ticket_closed' THEN event_time END) AS closed_at,
  TIMESTAMP_DIFF(MIN(CASE WHEN event_name = 'support_ticket_closed' THEN event_time END),
                 MIN(CASE WHEN event_name = 'support_ticket_opened' THEN event_time END), SECOND) AS time_to_resolution_seconds,
  COUNTIF(event_name = 'support_ticket_note') AS notes_count
FROM events
WHERE ticket_id IS NOT NULL
  AND DATE(event_time) BETWEEN DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 3 DAY) AND CURRENT_DATE()
GROUP BY ticket_id, account_id, severity, topic
ORDER BY FIELD(severity,'P0','P1') ASC, opened_at ASC

Error rate on critical endpoints
SQL (percentage of error events vs total events for those endpoints last 24 hours):

WITH critical AS (
  SELECT event_time, error_code
  FROM events
  WHERE event_time BETWEEN TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 24 HOUR) AND CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()
    AND endpoint IN ('/api/onboard','/api/activate','/api/charge') -- replace with your endpoints
)
SELECT
  COUNTIF(error_code IS NOT NULL) AS error_count,
  COUNT(*) AS total_requests,
  SAFE_DIVIDE(COUNTIF(error_code IS NOT NULL), COUNT(*)) AS error_rate
FROM critical

Active experiments & their status
Assumes you have an experiments table. If not, keep a manual list tile that Product updates.

Recent issues & action log (P0/P1)
Use the tickets SQL above filtered to severity P0/P1 and surface owner + ETA.

Visualization suggestions & sizing on Day‑0
- Header (full width): status + owner + last update
- Row 1 (four equal tiles): Activation rate 7d (big), DAU, Net New MRR (30d), D7 retention
- Row 2 (two wide tiles): Left — Funnel (hourly line + stacked counts) ; Right — MRR waterfall (stacked bar)
- Row 3 (wide): Cohort heatmap (D0–D30)
- Row 4 (two columns): Left — P0/P1 triage table (tickets) ; Right — Active experiments & actions list
- Footer: links to launch playbook, support FAQ, rollback steps

Alerts / thresholds to wire into dashboard or monitoring
- Activation funnel drop > 20% vs rolling 7-day avg — alert to product + eng
- Error rate > 2–5% on critical endpoints — paging to on-call
- > 10 launch-tagged support tickets/hour or any P0 ticket — urgent channel + exec notify
- Net New MRR negative in first 7 days — review customer issues/communications

Data freshness & ownership
- Real-time/minute-level for funnel & error tiles
- Hourly for DAU, tickets, MRR (billing events sometimes delayed — coordinate with billing)
- Owner roles:
  - Real-time monitoring owner: Analytics + On-call Eng Lead
  - Daily summary owner (first 7 days): Product (you)
  - Post-launch analysis owner: Product + Analytics

What I can hand next (pick one or both)

- Convert the SQL to your exact table/column names (you paste schema) or adapt to Snowflake/Redshift

Which would you like first? I can start by producing the LookML or a PNG mockup.

30/60/90-Day Plan (Senior Product Manager — start May 15)

Principles
- Learn fast, build trust, then execute.  
- Focus on customer outcomes and measurable impact.  
- Prioritize alignment with engineering, design, sales/CS, and execs.

First 30 days (May 15 – June 14): Learn & Observe
Goals
- Rapidly understand product, customers, team dynamics, and metrics.
- Build relationships and credibility.
Key activities
- Onboarding: get access to analytics, backlog, roadmap docs, OKRs, and customer research.
- Stakeholder map: meet with PM peers, Eng leads, Design lead, QA, Sales, CS, Marketing, and key execs (30–60 minute meetings).
- Data dive: review top product metrics (DAU/MAU, retention, conversion funnel, revenue, NPS, error rates).
- Team immersion: sit in sprint planning, standups, demos; review past retrospectives and decision logs.
- Customer exposure: join support/CS calls and run 3–5 customer interviews.
- Quick backlog review: identify technical debt and candidate quick wins.
Deliverables (end of 30 days)
- One-page product summary: metrics, top 3 opportunities, top risks.
- Stakeholder map with communication preferences.
- List of potential quick wins and experiments.
Success indicators
- Completed 1:1s with all direct reports and key stakeholders.
- Clear ownership boundaries and documented context for product area.
Risks & mitigations
- Risk: too many context asks, not enough delivery — mitigate by timeboxing discovery and scheduling delivery planning in week 3.

Days 31–60 (June 15 – July 14): Strategize & Align

We believe reducing required signup fields and offering social sign-in (Google/Apple/Facebook) will reduce early funnel friction, increasing activation rate and lowering time-to-activation. This experiment will compare baseline signup flow vs simplified flow with social sign-in and minimal fields.

- Security: review social sign-in compliance.

- Establish recurring cadences: weekly product sync, biweekly roadmap review, monthly stakeholder review.

Success metrics
- Aligned 90-day roadmap and metrics agreed with manager/stakeholders.
- At least one quick win launched or experiment running.
- Tracking dashboard reflecting agreed KPIs.

90 days — Deliver & scale
Goals
- Demonstrate measurable impact against agreed metrics.
- Cement processes for planning, delivery, and stakeholder communication.
- Coach and grow the team’s product capability.

Actions
- Drive delivery of committed milestones; remove blockers and ensure cross-functional coordination.

- Institutionalize rituals: weekly product demos, post-mortems, and a single source of truth for roadmap decisions.

Success metrics

- Roadmap delivery rate (e.g., % of committed milestones shipped).

Meeting cadence & practical templates
- Weekly: 30–60 min product sync (status, risks, decisions needed).

Delegation & time management

Common risks & mitigations
- Misalignment with stakeholders: run a short decision workshop and publish a single source of truth.
- Overcommitting: prioritize ruthlessly and define “must-have” vs “nice-to-have.”
- Team burnout: monitor velocity vs. capacity, ensure sustainable pacing and recognize wins.
- Lack of data: run rapid user interviews and tactical instrumentation for key funnels.

messages.content:
Love this — congrats again. Below is a customized 30/60/90 plan tuned to a 4-person team, growth-stage product, your top metrics (activation conversion, DAU/WAU retention, MRR), the ~8-week major feature launch, and the quarterly roadmap review at ~12 weeks. I also included a concise 30/60/90 one‑pager you can share and a ready-to-send team announcement. If you want, I can adapt wording to your voice or create a launch RACI/checklist next.

Customized 30/60/90 plan (high level)
Core priorities across 90 days
- Deliver the major feature on time and ensure it improves activation/retention/MRR.  
- Stabilize tracking and experiments so we can measure impact fast.  
- Align stakeholders and prepare a strong narrative for the quarterly roadmap review.

0–30 days — Listen, stabilize, and launch readiness
Objectives
- Build rapport and clear ownership across your 4-person team.  
- Confirm launch plan, technical readiness, and measurement requirements.  
- Identify 1–2 quick wins that improve activation or reduce friction pre-launch.

Actions
- 1:1s with each direct report (45–60m): clarify roles for launch, career goals, blockers, preferred communication.  
- Hold an immediate launch kickoff with Eng/Design/Data/CS: timeline, release criteria, roll-back plan. Make release owner explicit.  
- Audit instrumentation: ensure activation funnel, retention events, and revenue tracking are in place. Add missing events now.  
- Run a focused UX sweep on activation flows and top support tickets; scope any <2 week fixes as quick wins.  
- Prepare pre-launch comms (beta cohort invites, release notes, CS scripts).

Success metrics
- All launch acceptance criteria confirmed and owners assigned.  
- Instrumentation gaps closed for primary funnels.

31–60 days — Execute launch, measure early signal, iterate
Objectives
- Launch the feature (target ~week 8) with monitoring and experiment plan.  
- Capture early activation and retention signals and iterate quickly.  
- Align post-launch priorities that feed the quarterly review.

Actions
- Finalize QA, canary/beta plan, and release window; confirm rollback criteria.  
- Run pre-launch beta with a small cohort to validate activation and capture qualitative feedback.  
- Launch and monitor the dashboard closely for 72 hours, then daily for 2 weeks. Track activation conversion lift, DAU/WAU, and MRR impact.  
- Run at least one rapid experiment or A/B test tied to activation (e.g., onboarding flow tweak, messaging).  
- Host a post-launch readout within 7–10 days: initial metrics, top bugs, user feedback, recommended next steps.  
- Begin synthesizing learnings into the quarterly roadmap narrative.

Success metrics
- Feature released on schedule; no critical incidents; instrumentation captures key metrics.  
- Early lift (or hypothesis) on activation / retention identified OR clear next experiments defined.  
- Post-launch readout completed and circulated.

61–90 days — Show impact, institutionalize, and prepare roadmap review
Objectives
- Demonstrate measurable impact on at least one primary metric.  
- Create a clear 90-day outcomes report for the quarterly roadmap review.  
- Lock in ways of working for ongoing experimentation and delivery.

Actions
- Run/scale experiments that showed promise; stop/iterate on losers. Quantify impact on activation/retention/MRR.  
- Publish a 90-day outcomes doc (results vs. targets, learnings, recommended priorities for next quarter). Prepare slides for the roadmap review.  
- Institutionalize rituals: weekly product demo, decision log, and a single source of truth for roadmap decisions.  
- Do capability planning: identify any hiring/training needs to hit next-quarter targets.  
- Continue growth-focused 1:1s that coach direct reports on delivery and product thinking.

Success metrics
- Measurable improvement on at least one metric (e.g., +X% activation, improved retention cohort behavior, or incremental MRR), or a clear A/B winner with projected impact.  
- Roadmap review materials ready and aligned with stakeholders.  
- Regular cadence established and ownership delegated.

Who owns what (recommended for a 4-person cross-functional team)
- You (Senior PM): launch owner, stakeholder alignment, roadmap, prioritization, and measurement strategy.  
- Engineering lead(s): implementation, release process, monitoring/alerts.  
- Designer: onboarding/activation UX, post-launch UX tweaks, user testing.  
- Data/Analytics (or engineer with analytics responsibility): instrumentation, dashboards, experiment analysis.

Key risks and mitigations
- Measurement gaps — mitigate by instrumenting funnels in week 1–2.  
- Launch delays — run a weekly launch readiness checkpoint and define clear cutoffs.  
- No measurable lift — predefine primary hypotheses and backup experiments; plan to pivot within 2 weeks post-launch.  
- Team bandwidth — delegate execution work, free 20–30% of your time for cross-functional alignment.

30/60/90 one‑pager (copyable for Slack or doc)
Title: Senior PM 30/60/90 focus (growth-stage product, team of 4)
30 days — Learn & prepare

- Objectives: Show measurable metric improvement; prepare for quarterly roadmap review.

messages.content:
Great — I love this. Below are two deliverables you can use immediately:

1) Launch RACI (clear ownership) for the major feature
2) Detailed launch checklist (week-by-week, acceptance criteria, owners)

I assigned owners based on your team (you = Senior PM; Senior Backend Engineer = engineering lead; Frontend Engineer; Product Designer; Data Analyst). I also called out mitigations for the three technical risks you mentioned (incomplete instrumentation, scalability/performance, external auth/billing integration).

If you want, I can turn the slide content into a Google Slides / PowerPoint deck and export the launch checklist as a printable one-pager — tell me which format.

----------------------------------------------------------------
1) Launch RACI (high level)
Legend: R = Responsible (does the work), A = Accountable (final sign-off), C = Consulted, I = Informed

- Launch strategy, timeline, acceptance criteria
  - R: Senior PM
  - A: Senior PM
  - C: Eng Lead, Designer, Data Analyst
  - I: Stakeholders (Sales/CS, Marketing, Ops)

- Implementation (backend + frontend)
  - R: Senior Backend Engineer (backend work), Frontend Engineer (frontend work)
  - A: Senior Backend Engineer
  - C: Designer, Senior PM, Data Analyst
  - I: Team

- UX / Onboarding flows and copy
  - R: Product Designer
  - A: Product Designer
  - C: Senior PM, Frontend Engineer
  - I: Eng Lead

- Instrumentation & analytics (events, funnels, dashboards)
  - R: Data Analyst (implements/validates events), Engs implement event hooks
  - A: Data Analyst
  - C: Senior PM, Eng Lead
  - I: Stakeholders

- QA, load/performance testing
  - R: Eng Lead / Backend + Frontend Eng
  - A: Eng Lead
  - C: Senior PM, Data Analyst
  - I: Team

- Beta cohort management & qualitative feedback
  - R: Senior PM (coordination), CS/Support (shared) for outreach
  - A: Senior PM
  - C: Designer, Data Analyst
  - I: Eng Lead

- Release engineering (feature flagging, canary release, rollback)
  - R: Eng Lead
  - A: Eng Lead
  - C: Senior PM, Frontend Eng, Backend Eng
  - I: Team, Ops

- Monitoring & incident response / on-call during launch
  - R: Eng Lead + Backend Eng (monitoring); Senior PM to coordinate
  - A: Eng Lead
  - C: Data Analyst
  - I: Senior PM, Stakeholders

- External auth/billing integration coordination
  - R: Senior Backend Engineer (technical integration)
  - A: Senior Backend Engineer
  - C: Senior PM, Vendor contacts, Data Analyst (if billing metrics)
  - I: Legal/Finance if required

- Post-launch readout & next-experiments prioritization
  - R: Senior PM (compile), Data Analyst (metrics), Designer/Eng (input)
  - A: Senior PM
  - C: Stakeholders
  - I: Team

----------------------------------------------------------------
2) Launch checklist — timeline & acceptance criteria
(Assumes launch target ≈ week 8. Adjust week numbers to actual calendar.)

Pre-launch: Weeks 0–2 — Kickoff & instrumentation
- Kickoff meeting (within 48 hours)
  - Owner: Senior PM (R/A)
  - Acceptance: timeline, owners, rollback plan, communication plan documented and shared
- Instrumentation audit & gap-fix
  - Owner: Data Analyst (R), Engs implement event hooks
  - Acceptance: Activation funnel events, retention events, revenue events, error logging all defined and testable; test events visible in staging dashboard
- Define release criteria & feature flag plan
  - Owner: Senior PM (R), Eng Lead (C)
  - Acceptance: Checklist with go/no-go criteria, feature flags and canary rollout plan documented
- UX sweep for activation friction
  - Owner: Designer (R), Frontend Eng (C)
  - Acceptance: List of fixes prioritized; any <2-week fixes scheduled
- Identify beta cohort and communication plan
  - Owner: Senior PM (R), CS/Support (C)
  - Acceptance: 50–200 users (or relevant size) recruited, emails/templates ready

Weeks 3–5 — Build, QA, and instrumentation verification
- Development completed for core feature (backend + frontend)
  - Owner: Engs (R), Eng Lead (A)
  - Acceptance: All committed user stories done, unit/integration tests passing
- End-to-end testing: happy path + edge cases
  - Owner: Eng Lead (R), QA (if available) / Engs (C)
  - Acceptance: Test plan executed, bugs triaged <72h
- Load/performance testing
  - Owner: Eng Lead (R)
  - Acceptance: Baseline load test run (target concurrency), identify and fix critical bottlenecks; document acceptable thresholds
  - Mitigation: If failure, schedule priority performance sprint; escalate to PM for timeline impact
- Instrumentation validation in staging
  - Owner: Data Analyst (R), Engs (C)
  - Acceptance: Events appear in analytics, sample cohorts visible, dashboards populated with synthetic data
- Security & external integration check (auth/billing)
  - Owner: Senior Backend Engineer (R)
  - Acceptance: Integration handshake completed with vendor in staging; error handling paths validated; fallback plan documented (e.g., retry/backoff, offline flows)

Weeks 6–7 — Beta & pre-launch readiness
- Beta release to cohort
  - Owner: Senior PM (R), CS/Support (C)
  - Acceptance: Beta cohort usage tracked, qualitative issues logged; at least 1 round of feedback analyzed
- Pre-launch go/no-go review (1 week before)
  - Owner: Senior PM (R/A), Eng Lead (C), Data Analyst (C), Designer (C)
  - Acceptance: All go/no-go criteria green OR known issues with mitigation plan
- Finalize release notes, support scripts, monitoring playbook
  - Owner: Senior PM (R), CS/Support (C)
  - Acceptance: Docs published, support team trained
- Finalize rollback & emergency runbook
  - Owner: Eng Lead (R), Senior PM (C)
  - Acceptance: Step-by-step rollback validated in staging; notification list and channels defined

Week 8 — Launch week
- Canary / staged rollout (first window)
  - Owner: Eng Lead (R), Senior PM (A)
  - Acceptance: No critical errors, key metrics monitored (first 72h)
- Monitor 0–72 hours intensively
  - Owner: Eng Lead (R for infra), Data Analyst (R for metrics), Senior PM (R for coordination)
  - Acceptance: Error rate below threshold, latency within SLA, no major negative user feedback
- If issues: execute rollback plan or hotfix
  - Owner: Eng Lead (R)
  - Acceptance: Rollback executed within defined SLA OR hotfix deployed and validated

Post-launch: Weeks 9–12 — Early signal & iteration
- Post-launch readout (within 7–10 days)
  - Owner: Senior PM (R), Data Analyst (C)
  - Acceptance: Metrics snapshot (activation, DAU/WAU, early MRR signal), top 5 issues, user quotes, recommended next steps
- A/B test(s) and rapid experiments begun
  - Owner: Senior PM (R), Designer (R for UX variations), Data Analyst (R for analysis)
  - Acceptance: Experiment running with sample size/visibility, expected metric to measure defined
- Scale or stop experiments based on data (weeks 10–12)
  - Owner: Senior PM + Data Analyst (R/A)
  - Acceptance: Decision log with winners/losers and follow-up actions
- Prepare quarter-review materials
  - Owner: Senior PM (R), Data Analyst (C), Eng Lead (C)
  - Acceptance: Slide deck (see below) and 90-day outcomes doc ready before roadmap review

Ongoing monitoring & ops
- On-call rota for critical first 72 hours (and a lighter watch for next 2 weeks)
  - Owner: Eng Lead (R), Senior PM (I)
  - Acceptance: Roster published, alert thresholds confirmed
- Instrumentation runbook for new events
  - Owner: Data Analyst (R)
  - Acceptance: Catalog of events with owners, definitions, and dashboard mapping

Critical acceptance criteria to track at all times
- Instrumentation: events flowing into analytics and dashboards match expected counts in staging
- Performance: latency and error budgets respected under expected load
- External dependency: integration success/failure rates within acceptable SLA; fallback routes validated
- Business: activation funnel baseline vs. expected delta, early retention cohort trends monitored, MRR tracking validated

----------------------------------------------------------------
3) Draft quarterly roadmap slide deck (12 slides) — content + speaker notes
I’ve written suggested content for each slide. Replace placeholder numbers with your real baselines when available.

Slide 1 — Title
- Title: Quarterly Roadmap Review — [Product]
- Subtitle: Launch status, outcomes, and priorities for next quarter
- Presenter: [Your name], Senior Product Manager
Speaker note: Quick hello, goal of the session (align on outcomes, decisions, and resourcing).

Slide 2 — Agenda
- Quick summary & asks
- Key metrics & baseline
- Launch status & timeline
- Post-launch results & learnings
- Next-quarter priorities and roadmap
- Resourcing & risks
- Decisions / asks
Speaker note: Explain timing and decision points.

Slide 3 — Executive summary (1-slide elevator)
- One-sentence summary of launch status: e.g., “Feature launched on [date]; instrumentation validated; initial activation lift of X% (or: early signal pending).”
- Top 3 asks (examples): 1) Approve 0.5 FTE Data Engineering to finish instrumentation, 2) Budget approval for performance optimization sprint, 3) Approval to proceed with prioritized experiments
Speaker note: State the overall outcome and 2–3 things you need from leadership.

Slide 4 — Key metrics (before & target)
- Table / bullets with current baseline and target for the quarter:
  - Activation conversion: baseline X% → target X+Y%
  - Retention (DAU/WAU ratio and 7d retention): baseline → target
  - MRR: baseline → target
- Visual suggestion: small bar chart or trend sparkline for each metric
Speaker note: Call out what success looks like and why these matter for growth.

Slide 5 — Launch timeline & status
- Visual timeline: kickoff → beta → launch (week ~8) → post-launch readout → roadmap review (week ~12)
- Status bullets: dev complete (date), instrumentation status (green/yellow/red), performance testing status
Speaker note: Make clear what is done, in-progress, and any slippages.

Slide 6 — Launch results (initial signals)
- Metrics (replace with real numbers): Activation delta, new user onboarding completion %, DAU/WAU change for affected cohorts, initial incremental MRR if available
- Operational signals: error rate, rollback events, support tickets (count), performance metrics
- Quick user feedback bullets from beta
Speaker note: Emphasize early wins or explain if metrics are neutral/negative and the plan for experiments.

Slide 7 — What we learned / top issues
- Top 3 learnings (e.g., onboarding copy confusion, certain cohort shows better retention, external auth failures for 2% of users)
- Top 3 issues to address (with owners and ETA)
Speaker note: Show that you captured learnings and have clear owners for mitigations.

Slide 8 — Proposed priorities for next quarter (RICE-ranked)
- Priority 1 (e.g., Scale experiments that improved activation) — impact, owner, timeline
- Priority 2 (e.g., Performance optimization to meet 99th percentile latency target)
- Priority 3 (e.g., Complete instrumentation & add revenue attribution)
- Include RICE scores or short rationale
Speaker note: Ask for alignment on these priorities and mention trade-offs.

Slide 9 — Roadmap view (next 90 days)
- Visual roadmap timeline with 3 swimlanes: Product (experiments/feature iterations), Engineering (perf, integration), Analytics (dashboards/experiments)
- Milestones: experiment launches, scaling winners, perf sprint, auth/billing hardening
Speaker note: Explain deliverables and how they map to metrics.

Slide 10 — Resourcing & dependencies
- Current team capacity (4 people) and constraints
- Requests: e.g., temporary Data Engineering support, 1 sprint of backend performance engineering, vendor SLA negotiation help
- External dependencies: vendor timelines for auth/billing
Speaker note: Make clear what you need to hit targets.

Slide 11 — Risks & mitigations (explicit)
- Instrumentation gaps: Mitigation = priority instrumentation sprint (owner: Data Analyst + Engs)
- Scalability/performance: Mitigation = load testing + dedicated perf sprint; monitor and on-call during release (owner: Eng Lead)
- External auth/billing integration: Mitigation = vendor coordination, fallback UX/queueing, contract/SLAs (owner: Senior Backend Engineer + Senior PM)
- New risk: capacity for parallel experiments — mitigation: focus on top 1–2 experiments
Speaker note: Ask for support on any organizational mitigations required.

Slide 12 — Decisions & asks
- Be explicit (examples):
  - Decision 1: Approve temporary 0.5 FTE Data Engineering for instrumentation (cost + timeline)
  - Decision 2: Approve one-week performance bugfix sprint (scope & priority)
  - Decision 3: Approve go-forward list of top 3 experiments for next quarter
- Next steps and owners
Speaker note: Close with a short timeline for decisions and availability for follow-ups.

Appendix slides (optional)
- Detailed instrumentation mapping (events & owners)
- Full launch checklist & runbook
- Data definitions & cohort methodology
- Incident logs and rollback procedures

----------------------------------------------------------------
Immediate next steps I can take (pick any)
- Convert the deck content into a Google Slides/PowerPoint file and populate a launch timeline visual.
- Produce the launch checklist as a printable one-pager (PDF/Google Doc).
- Create the runbook templates: post-launch readout template, incident playbook, and decision log.
- Fill the deck with real metrics if you paste baseline numbers for activation, retention, and MRR.

Which of these would you like me to do next? Also tell me if you want the RACI exported as a sheet (CSV) for easy sharing.

  - Announce your new role to the team and stakeholders (offer to share goals and hold a kickoff).
  - Block 1:1s with each direct report, the Engineering Manager, Design Lead, QA/Eng, Head of Product (your manager), Customer Success, Analytics, Marketing, and Sales — schedule these for first 2–3 weeks.
  - Get access to dashboards, analytics, backlog, roadmap, KPIs, and main product/infra tickets.
- Triage & listening
  - Run a 30–60 minute “current state” review with team: current onboarding funnel metrics, recent releases, major blockers.
  - Pull baseline metrics for onboarding: new-user activation rate, time-to-first-value, step-by-step drop-off, A/B experiments, support ticket volume for onboarding issues.
- One quick win
  - Ship one low-effort improvement (e.g., tweak welcome email CTA, clarify first-screen copy, reduce a nonessential signup field) that you can measure within 7 days.

30-day plan — learn, stabilize, get early wins
Objectives
- Understand root causes of slow onboarding and delivery blockers.
- Deliver one measurable onboarding improvement.
- Establish regular cross-functional rituals.

Key activities
- Onboarding audit (deep dive)
  - Map the onboarding journey: account creation → activation → first key action.
  - Analyze conversion funnels by cohort, device, channel.
  - Run qualitative research: observe 5–10 new users, review support transcripts, interview CS and Sales.
  - Audit product analytics events to ensure instrumentation covers activation points.
- Backlog & roadmap triage
  - Triage onboarding-related backlog and categorize: quick-fix, experiment, product change, platform change.
  - Prioritize top 3 onboarding initiatives and create success metrics for each.
- Cross-functional alignment
  - Set weekly cross-functional sync (30–45m) with Eng, Design, CS, Analytics, Marketing to unblock delivery and align on priorities.
  - Define a single source of truth for status (Jira board/Confluence page).
- Delivery improvements (early)
  - Introduce or tighten Definition of Done (DoD) and acceptance criteria for onboarding tasks.
  - Implement a lightweight PR/release checklist for onboarding changes.
- Metrics and targets
  - Establish baseline metrics and target improvements (example targets below).

Deliverables by day 30
- Onboarding audit report with prioritized backlog (top 3 initiatives).
- Measurement plan: events, dashboards, and A/B test plan.
- Weekly cross-functional meeting cadence established.
- One measurable quick win shipped and monitored.

60-day plan — act and iterate
Objectives
- Start delivering the prioritized initiatives and iterate based on data.
- Improve cross‑functional delivery speed and predictability.

Key activities
- Run experiments
  - Launch A/B tests for prioritized onboarding flows (e.g., reduced steps vs current flow, guided tour vs none).
  - Track activation, time-to-first-value, retention for cohorts.
- Process improvements for delivery
  - Implement a lightweight intake/template for new feature requests (one-page brief: problem, user, success metrics, risks).
  - Introduce weekly prioritization grooming with Eng and Design to keep sprint queues healthy.
  - Run stricter sprint retros focusing on cycle time, blockers, and action items; measure cycle time reductions.
  - Start using a RACI for onboarding projects to remove ambiguity.
- Strengthen cross-functional ownership
  - Co-own success metrics with CS/Marketing for first-week retention and activation.
  - Run monthly stakeholder review demo and metric review (30–45m).
- People and team health
  - Continue 1:1s; set development objectives with each direct report.
  - Identify any skill gaps and begin arranging training or hires if needed.

Deliverables by day 60
- Two or more experiments launched with early readouts.
- Documented intake process, DoD, and sprint improvements in Confluence.
- Measurable improvement: e.g., 10–20% lift in activation or 20% reduction in average time-to-first-value (targets depend on baseline).

90-day plan — deliver and scale
Objectives
- Demonstrate measurable onboarding gains and a smoother delivery process.
- Lock in a roadmap for next 6–12 months based on validated learning.

Key activities
- Evaluate experiments and scale winners
  - Ramp up successful variants from experiments into full rollouts.
  - Archive learnings and failures; iterate on failed experiments.
- Roadmap & OKRs
  - Propose a 6–12 month onboarding roadmap aligned with company objectives.
  - Set 2–3 clear OKRs (examples below).
- Cross-functional maturity
  - Institutionalize the weekly sync, monthly metric review, and release checklist.
  - Ensure analytics coverage and SLAs for onboarding bugs and regressions.
- Team enablement
  - Run a workshop to share learnings and best practices across teams.

Deliverables by day 90
- Documented roadmap + prioritized backlog for next 6–12 months.
- Demonstrable metric improvements (activation, time-to-first-value, retention).
- Continued improved delivery predictability (reduced cycle time, fewer rollbacks).

Suggested KPIs / success metrics
- Activation rate (e.g., % of new users completing key activation step within 7 days).
- Time-to-first-value (median hours/days until user achieves core value).
- 7-day and 30-day retention for new cohorts.
- Onboarding completion rate / drop-off at each funnel step.
- Support tickets related to onboarding (volume & time-to-resolution).
- Cycle time for onboarding features (idea → production).
- % of sprints delivered on committed scope.

Example OKRs (customize targets after baselines)
- Objective: Faster, frictionless onboarding
  - KR1: Increase 7-day activation from X% → X+15%.
  - KR2: Reduce median time-to-first-value from Y days → Y*0.7.
  - KR3: Reduce onboarding support tickets by 30%.
- Objective: More predictable cross-functional delivery
  - KR1: Reduce average cycle time for onboarding features by 25%.
  - KR2: 90% of releases meet DoD and pass acceptance criteria.
  - KR3: Hold weekly cross-functional syncs with 95% attendance and documented outcomes.

Quick-win ideas you can implement in week 1–4
- Reduce friction in signup: remove nonessential fields, enable social sign-in.
- Improve first-run experience: add a single interactive tip that guides to the value.
- Better email onboarding: sequence that drives activation within first 24–48 hours.
- Pre-fill or smart defaults for setup steps.
- “Help while you go” microcopy and inline contextual CTAs.
- Triage and fix the top 3 onboarding bugs causing most customer support volume.

Cross-functional delivery checklist / practices
- Clear intake: one-page brief with success metrics and stakeholders.
- DoD and acceptance criteria attached to every ticket.
- Weekly prioritization and backlog grooming session.
- Short daily standups and a weekly cross-functional unblock meeting.
- Feature toggles for risky rollouts and canary releases.
- Post-release monitoring and a rollback plan.
- Sprint retros with a follow-up tracker on action items.

1:1 template for first meeting with direct reports (30–45m)
- Quick personal intro + how they prefer to work (5m).
- Current priorities and biggest blockers (10m).
- What’s going well and what they’d change about onboarding/delivery (10m).
- Career & support: what they want to learn or need from you (10m).
- Agree on next steps and follow-up (5m).

Stakeholder map (who to prioritize)
- Engineering Manager — delivery capacity & technical debt.
- Design Lead / UX — onboarding flows and usability.
- Analytics / Data Team — event instrumentation and dashboards.
- Customer Success / Support — qualitative feedback and pain points.
- Marketing — acquisition channels and welcome messaging.
- Sales — first-week user experience for demo-to-customer conversion.
- QA — regression & release confidence.
- Security/Legal — compliance relevant to onboarding.

Risks and mitigations
- Risk: Too many parallel initiatives dilute impact — Mitigation: prioritize top 3 and guard team focus.
- Risk: Incomplete instrumentation — Mitigation: make measurement plan a blocker for shipping.
- Risk: Stakeholder misalignment — Mitigation: early stakeholder kickoff and documented RACI.
- Risk: Quick fixes mask deeper UX problems — Mitigation: combine quick wins with experiments and qualitative research.

Templates I can draft for you (ready to customize)
- Announcement email to announce role and first objectives.
- 30–60–90 slide or doc you can share with manager/team.
- One-page intake template and PR/release checklist.
- 1:1 agenda and feedback tracker.
- Onboarding audit template and analytics event checklist.

Want me to: 
- Draft the announcement email and your first-week schedule? 
- Or build the 30–60–90 in a shareable slide/doc format (I can produce plain text you can copy into Slides/Confluence)?

1) Concise announcement / thank-you (for team/all-hands or email)
Subject: Excited to step into the Senior Product Manager role

2) Short thank-you note to your manager/mentor
Hi [Name], thank you so much for your support and guidance — it means a lot. I’m excited for the opportunity and committed to delivering impact. Could we schedule a 30-minute check-in this week to align expectations and priorities for my first 90 days?

— [Your name]

30/60/90-day plan (Senior Product Manager) — high-level, actionable

Goals (overall)
- Build credibility and relationships
- Understand product, customers, and metrics deeply
- Deliver early, visible wins and set a clear roadmap

First 30 days — Learn & connect (listen more than act)
- Meet: 1:1s with direct reports, product partners (engineering, design), key stakeholders, and 5–8 top customers or CS reps.
- Audit: product metrics (DAU/MAU, retention, conversion), OKRs, backlog health, active experiments, major tech/UX debt.
- Observe: release cadence, sprint process, decision-making framework.
- Quick wins: fix 1–2 low-effort visible issues (triage critical bugs, unblock a stalled PR, clarify a confusing KPI).
- Deliverable: 30-day summary: stakeholder map, top 3 product risks/opportunities, proposed priorities.

Success metrics for 30 days:
- 100% of key stakeholder 1:1s completed
- Clear list of top 3 risks/opps and immediate quick wins identified

Days 31–60 — Align & prioritize
- Synthesize findings into strategy options and draft roadmap themes (customer value + business impact).
- Run prioritization sessions with stakeholders (use RICE/ICE or custom framework), decide top initiatives for next 3–6 months.
- Improve processes: stabilize grooming, strengthen definition of ready/done, introduce a lightweight decision log.
- Start work on top-priority initiative(s) with cross-functional owners.
- Deliverable: prioritized 90-day roadmap, KPIs for each initiative, communication plan.

Success metrics for 60 days:
- Agreed prioritized backlog and roadmap themes
- Active cross-functional plan for top initiative(s) with owners and timelines

Days 61–90 — Execute & measure
- Drive delivery of top initiatives; remove blockers and ensure strong communication/coordination.
- Establish a cadence for progress reviews (weekly syncs, monthly metrics review).
- Define/measure outcome KPIs (activation, retention, revenue, NPS) and report early results.
- Institutionalize improvements: hiring/training needs, playbooks, OKR alignment.
- Deliverable: 90-day review with results vs. KPIs, updated 6-month roadmap, recommendations.

Success metrics for 90 days:
- First initiative(s) shipped or in late-stage rollout
- Measurable improvement in at least one target KPI
- Stakeholder alignment and documented roadmap

Risks & mitigations
- Risk: moving too fast without buy-in — Mitigation: prioritize stakeholder alignment sessions and transparent decision criteria.

First one-on-ones with direct reports — agenda and talking points
Aim for 45–60 minutes for first meetings. Purpose: listen more than speak, build trust, set expectations, identify immediate issues.

Suggested agenda (45–60 mins)

2. Their story (10–15 mins)

3. Current priorities & blockers (10–15 mins)
   - What are your top projects? What’s blocking progress?
4. Team & process feedback (8–10 mins)
   - What’s working well? What should change?
5. Career & support (8–10 mins)
   - What are your career goals? How can I support you?
6. Commitments & next steps (3–5 mins)

Key questions to ask (listen, probe, and take notes)

Three quick‑win experiment briefs
Note: timings are suggested; adjust after baseline metrics and power calculations.

Experiment A — Post‑signup onboarding email sequence
- Title: 3‑message onboarding email sequence to drive first meaningful action
- Owner: PM-A (design: Designer; analytics: Analyst; build: Eng)
- Hypothesis: Sending a tailored 3‑message onboarding email series in the first 72 hours will increase activation (signup → activation) vs control because it reduces time‑to‑first‑value and guides users to the key action.
- Primary metric: Activation rate (signup → activation within 7 days)
- Secondary metrics: Time‑to‑first‑value (median), email open rate, CTR to activation flow, Day‑7 retention
- Design: Randomized A/B test (50/50) where test group receives email series; control receives current baseline (no sequence or existing single email).
- Instrumentation:
  - Track email sends/opens/clicks
  - Track event for "activation" and timestamp
  - Cohort tagging for test/control
- Sample & duration: Run for N full cohorts or 2–4 weeks (ensure statistical power before full rollout)
- Success criteria: Statistically significant lift in activation (pre-defined delta, e.g., +10% relative) with no negative impact on Day‑7 retention or increase in spam complaints.
- Risks / mitigations: Low opens — iterate subject lines; if CTR low, change CTA to more obvious first action.
- Next steps (first 72h):
  1. PM drafts email copy + CTA (owner)
  2. Designer creates simple template
  3. Analyst sets up cohorts & tracking
  4. Eng implements email send and hooks
  5. Launch & monitor daily

Experiment B — Simplify signup/onboarding flow (remove optional step)
- Title: Reduced-step signup flow (hide optional step X)
- Owner: PM-B (design: Designer; analytics: Analyst; build: Eng)
- Hypothesis: Removing one optional step that currently causes drop-off will reduce time‑to‑first‑value and increase activation by decreasing friction.
- Primary metric: Activation rate (signup → activation)
- Secondary metrics: Drop-off rate at step X, time-to-first-value, onboarding completion
- Design: A/B test (control = current flow; variant = flow with step removed or deferred)
- Instrumentation:
  - Events for each step in signup/onboarding
  - Time stamps to compute TTFV
  - Cohort assignment
- Sample & duration: 2–3 weeks or until 1,000–2,000 users per arm depending on traffic
- Success criteria: Significant reduction in drop-off at step X and net increase in activation without increasing downstream support tickets
- Risks / mitigations: If step is needed for compliance or data later, defer to post-activation capture; ensure no missing required data.
- Next steps:
  1. PM identifies step to remove + justification
  2. Designer mocks variant
  3. Analyst configures funnel events
  4. Eng implements feature flag and variant
  5. Run, analyze, decide to roll forward or revert

Experiment C — In‑app onboarding checklist / guided tour
- Title: In‑product checklist that drives first 3 actions
- Owner: PM-C (design: Designer; analytics: Analyst; build: Eng)
- Hypothesis: Exposing an in-app checklist of the first 3 meaningful actions increases onboarding completion and improves Day‑7 retention because users know exactly what to do next.
- Primary metric: Onboarding completion rate (checklist completion)
- Secondary metrics: Activation rate, Day‑7 retention, checklist interaction rate
- Design: Feature-flagged rollout to a randomized cohort (gradual rollout preferred)
- Instrumentation:
  - Events for checklist shown, item clicked, item completed, completion timestamp
  - Link to retention cohorts
- Sample & duration: Start with 10% of new users for 1 week, ramp to 50% if signals positive; total test 3–4 weeks
- Success criteria: Increase in checklist completion and corresponding lift in activation/Day‑7 retention; no increased confusion or feature abandonment
- Risks / mitigations: UX clutter — keep checklist minimal and dismissible; measure negative engagement signals and be ready to iterate.
- Next steps:
  1. Designer prototypes minimal checklist
  2. PM defines 3 highest‑leverage actions
  3. Analyst sets events and dashboards
  4. Eng builds under feature flag
  5. Launch to small cohort, monitor, iterate

30/60/90 plan (Senior Product Manager — start June 1)

Overall goals: build credibility quickly, align on priorities, deliver early wins, and establish durable team rhythms.

Days 31–60 — Start delivering and set direction (Execution)
- Objectives
  - Get early outcomes from quick wins, propose prioritized roadmap, and create clarity on roles/ownership.
- Key actions

  - Kick off quick-win projects and remove blockers (weekly check-ins).
  - Clarify product ownership, decision rights, and communication cadence (e.g., weekly priorities doc; monthly roadmap sync).

  - Measure and share results of quick wins; iterate based on data.
  - Finalize roadmap for next 6–12 months; get leadership sign-off where needed.
  - Hold one or more team workshops to codify working norms, career paths, and feedback loops.
  - Create development plans for direct reports and identify hiring needs.
  - Present a 90-day outcomes report to manager/leadership.

  - 90-day report: outcomes vs. baseline, validated roadmap, team development plan, next steps.

  - Clear KPI improvements, stakeholder buy-in for roadmap, strengthened team morale and clarity.

Practical tactics for leading former peers
- Acknowledge the transition: in your first team meeting say you value previous working relationships and expect to work differently to support the team.
- Be transparent about priorities and decision-making; ambiguity breeds distrust.
- Balance humility and authority: ask for input, but make timely decisions when needed.
- Delegate outcomes, not just tasks: specify the goal, success metrics, and level of autonomy.

B. Tough conversation with a former peer who resists direction — scripts & approach
Principles to use in the conversation
- Lead with curiosity and respect; name the relationship shift explicitly.
- Link behaviors to business impact (not personality).
- Be clear about expectations and decision rights.
- Offer support and invite options/solutions from them.
- Document agreements and follow up.

Script — opening (first conversation)
“Thanks for meeting. I value everything we accomplished together and I want to be upfront: I know this is a shift from peer → manager, and I want to understand how you’re feeling about that. I’ve noticed [specific behavior: e.g., you’ve pushed back in planning meetings or continued directing the roadmap]. Can you help me understand your perspective?”

If they explain concerns, acknowledge:
“I hear you — that’s a fair point about [concern]. My job now is to make tradeoffs across the product and ensure we hit these outcomes: [share 1–2 priority metrics]. That means I need alignment on decisions in [area].”

State the desired behavior and rationale (clear ask)
“Concretely, I need you to [do X; stop doing Y]. For example: when we decide to prioritize feature A, I need you to focus your team on delivery and raise alternatives with data before the prioritization meeting — not after a decision has been communicated. That helps us move faster and keeps the team aligned.”

If they push back or resist
“I hear you’re uncomfortable with that. Tell me what would make this workable. If your concern is that we’re missing something, bring a concise alternative with impact estimates and we’ll evaluate it in the forum. I’m open to changing a decision if it’s the best option, but once we choose a path I expect the team to execute.”

If resistance continues after agreement (follow-up / accountability)
“I appreciate the conversation last week and the commitments you made. I’ve noticed [specific example of not following through]. That is blocking team progress and undermines alignment. We need to agree on immediate steps: 1) you’ll [specific action] by [date]; 2) I’ll support by [resource or support]. If this continues, we’ll need to escalate and revisit roles to ensure we can meet our goals.”

Short escalation language (if needed)
“I don’t want this to get to escalation, but I need reliable execution to meet our commitments. If we can’t align on how to work together, I’ll have to involve [manager/HR] to reset expectations.”

Closing and follow-up (always document)
“Thanks for being candid. To confirm: you’ll do [X], I’ll do [Y], and we’ll check back on [date]. I’ll send a short note summarizing this so we both have it.”

After the meeting: send a brief email summary with agreed actions, timelines, and the date of the next check-in.

Quick tactical tips
- Use one concrete example of the problematic behavior — avoid vague complaints.
- Don’t surprise them in public; always have the first hard conversation in private.
- Give them a way to influence decisions constructively (present alternatives with data).
- If they’re influential and repeatedly obstructive, track consequences and timeline before escalating.

- Use the KPI cards visually to anchor each metric you mention — point to the slide.

A. First 1:1 with a direct report (30–45 min)

30/60/90 plan (tailored)

30 days — Learn, stabilize the release, unblock hires
Goals
- Lock scope and immediate plan for the Q3 feature beta (in ~6 weeks).
- Stop new scope creep, reduce high‑risk technical blockers, open hiring pipeline.
- Establish relationships and alignment with VP Product, Eng Lead, Sales, and CS.

Activities / concrete actions
- Run a 1–2 hour scope lock session with Eng Lead + core contributors: confirm MVP for beta, list must‑have vs nice‑to‑have items, identify any blockers. Owner: you + Eng Lead.
- Create a clear beta success criteria doc (metrics, acceptance tests, beta cohort). Owner: you.
- Triage technical debt items that block the beta; classify P0 (blockers), P1 (high), P2 (nice). Agree with Eng Lead to reserve ~15–25% sprint capacity for P0/P1 fixes. Owner: Eng Lead / you.
- Start hiring urgently: raise job req for full‑stack engineer, draft interview loop (tech screen, pair exercise on product bug/feature, culture interview), ask Eng Lead for referrals and contractors as stopgap. Owner: you + Eng Lead.
- Run churn quick analysis: top cohorts, exit reasons (CS/Surveys, product usage data). Owner: you + Head of CS / analytics.
- Hold 1:1s with each direct report and key stakeholders to gather expectations and risks (use the scripts below).

Deliverables / success metrics
- Beta scope locked and published; rollout plan with owners and dates.

- Job req opened + initial candidate pipeline or approved contract option.
- Churn hypothesis list (top 3 drivers) and one proposed quick mitigation.

60 days — Execute beta, show quick wins, hire pipeline
Goals
- Launch beta on schedule; gather qualitative and quantitative feedback.

- Progress hiring to interviews / offer stage.

Activities / concrete actions
- Execute beta launch activities: QA run, instrumentation for analytics, communication to beta users, CS support flow, rollback plan. Owner: you + Eng Lead + Head of CS.

- Implement 1–2 quick wins from churn analysis (e.g., onboarding tweak, improved in‑app messaging, priority bug fix) and measure impact. Owner: you + Head of CS + Engineering.
- Continue hiring: screen candidates, run paired live exercise with Eng Lead, target offer by week 8–10 or contract start as fallback.

90 days — GA, scale, long‑term prioritization

- Propose and socialize an ongoing prioritization framework (RICE/ICE + strategic bets) and mapping of roadmap to company objectives. Owner: you.

- Hire onboarded / contractor transitioned, team health check and development plan for direct reports.

- Published roadmap and prioritization framework with VP Product buy‑in.
- Hiring closed or contractor running; engineering capacity stable.
- Early metric improvements (examples: activation +X%, churn down Y% — define targets with VP Product).

Risks & mitigation
- Risk: Beta slips due to tech debt. Mitigate: reserve capacity for blockers, escalate early in weekly syncs; push non‑critical scope.
- Risk: Hiring delays. Mitigate: contractor fallback, expedite referrals, hire for core skillset first.
- Risk: Stakeholder misalignment. Mitigate: weekly targeted updates and shared success criteria for feature.

Suggested KPIs to track (discuss numeric targets with VP Product)
- Beta health: error/bug rate, crash rate, feature activation %, beta user retention after 7/30 days.
- Churn indicators: monthly churn rate, NPS/CSAT for at‑risk cohorts, top‑exit reasons.
- Delivery: % of planned scope shipped on schedule, mean time to resolve critical bugs.
- Team: time-to-hire for full‑stack role, team satisfaction pulse.

First 1:1 with your manager (VP Product) — 30–45 min

30-60-90 Day Plan (Senior Product Manager) — goals, actions, and quick wins

Overall focus: quickly build credibility by listening and shipping a few high-impact improvements, align stakeholders around a clear roadmap, and establish a repeatable process for team development and cross-functional delivery.

0–30 days — Listen, learn, stabilize
Goals

- Launch team development initiatives: monthly lunch-and-learn, office hours, or shadowing sessions.

- One shipped quick-win with impact report
- Decision log and published KPIs

60–90 days — Execute, measure, and scale

- Deliver on a larger roadmap milestone and show measurable impact.
- Institutionalize processes for cross-functional alignment and team growth.
- Coach and grow the product team’s capability.

Actions / Quick wins
- Deliver first larger milestone or major feature iteration and present impact vs baseline.
- Publish a 3–6 month roadmap + communicate to the org (include success metrics).
- Run a retrospective on the first 90 days: what worked, what to change.
- Develop individual development plans for direct reports and set mentoring cadence (e.g., monthly career check-ins).
- Propose improvements to product development cycle (triage, planning, QA, release).
