Nice — congrats again. Below is a concrete, role-specific 30/60/90-day plan for your first 90 days as Senior Product Manager, Platform, plus ready-to-use talking points and questions for your one-on-one with your manager.

30/60/90-Day Plan — Senior Product Manager, Platform

Guiding principles
- Focus on outcomes, not activity: prioritize work that increases platform reliability, developer productivity, and adoption.
- Balance short-term credibility (quick wins) with medium-term strategic bets (scalable improvements).
- Make decisions visible: baseline metrics, hypotheses, and a clear escalation path.

30 days — Assess, learn, and get early wins
Objectives
- Rapidly understand product, people, and tech: where the platform helps or blocks product teams.
- Build relationships and credibility with engineers, product peers, SRE, design, security, and key internal customers.
- Identify 2–3 immediate quick wins with measurable impact.

Actions
- Meet: 1:1 with every direct report, tech leads, SRE, infra, key PM peers, head of engineering, customer success, a couple of exec stakeholders.
- Read: platform roadmap, architecture diagrams, incident retros, backlog, SLAs/SLOs, onboarding docs, support tickets, deployment cadence.
- Metrics deep-dive: current uptime/SLA, error rate, API latency, MTTR, developer onboarding time, platform API adoption, backlog size, cycle time.
- Run a “platform health” session: share initial observations and solicit input.
- Ship one quick win (example options): fix a high-impact recurring bug, improve developer onboarding docs or sample apps, add a small dashboard or alert to reduce noise.

Deliverables (end of 30 days)
- 30-day summary: current state, top 3 risks/opportunities, proposed quick wins and owners.
- Immediate action plan for the quick wins and a proposed 60-day focus.

Success criteria
- Completed 1:1s with direct reports and key partners.
- Baseline metrics captured.
- At least 1 quick win shipped or in-flight.

60 days — Strategize, prioritize, and align
Objectives
- Define platform goals and metrics for the next 3–6 months; align stakeholders.
- Tackle prioritized technical debt or product work that unlocks the most developer productivity or reliability gains.
- Improve processes (release, incident, onboarding) that reduce friction.

Actions
- Build a prioritized roadmap (30–90 day outcomes) tied to measurable KPIs (SLOs, adoption, dev velocity).
- Negotiate and secure resources: engineering focus, tooling, budgets.
- Introduce/standardize runbooks, incident response improvements, onboarding flows, or platform SDKs.
- Start a pilot for a larger initiative (e.g., internal developer portal improvements, API versioning strategy, automated CI/CD templates).

Deliverables (end of 60 days)
- 60-day report + proposed 90-day roadmap and OKRs/metrics.
- Cross-functional sign-off on priorities and resourcing.
- Two process changes or automation improvements implemented.

Success criteria
- Stakeholder alignment on priorities.
- First measurable improvements in at least one target metric (e.g., reduced onboarding time by X%, decreased P1 incidents).
- Clear resource plan and timeline for larger platform initiatives.

90 days — Execute, measure, and scale
Objectives
- Deliver on a major platform initiative or measurable set of improvements.
- Institutionalize cadence and visibility: dashboards, reporting, and review rituals.
- Set hiring/structure recommendations if needed.

Actions
- Complete and ship the prioritized initiative(s).
- Review progress against 30/60/90 OKRs; iterate.
- Propose org or resourcing changes (hiring, contractors, rotation plans).
- Create long-term roadmap and risk register.

Deliverables (end of 90 days)
- 90-day report: before/after metrics, lessons learned, recommended next-quarter roadmap and hires.
- Documented platform operating model: owner matrix, SLAs, incident playbooks, release process.
- Demonstrable improvement to targeted metrics (developer adoption, MTTR, SLA compliance, etc.).

Success criteria
- Measurable improvement on 1–3 agreed KPIs vs baseline.
- Positive stakeholder feedback and clear next-quarter plan.
- Team morale and velocity stabilized or improved.

Suggested metrics to track
- Reliability: uptime, SLO compliance, MTTR, number of P1 incidents.

Subject: New role — Senior Product Manager, Growth

Hi all,

I’m excited to share that I’ve stepped into the Senior Product Manager role for the Growth squad. In this role I’ll own growth strategy and the squad roadmap, mentor our three product managers, and drive cross‑functional alignment with Eng, Data, Marketing, and Customer Success. 30/60/90-day plan (focused, actionable)

High-level theme per phase:
- 0–30 days: Learn & align — understand team, processes, metrics, and stakeholders; build credibility.
- 31–60 days: Stabilize & deliver — pick early bets, run experiments, set initial priorities and rituals.
- 61–90 days: Scale & lead — institutionalize processes, measure impact, coach PMs for ownership, set medium-term roadmap.

30-day goals — Learn & align
- Objectives:
  - Rapidly learn product, metrics, current experiments, backlog, and team strengths.
  - Build relationships with PMs, Eng leads, Data, Marketing, Sales, CS, and your manager.
- Key activities:
  - One-on-ones with each direct report (weekly recurring) + 30–60 min discovery with each PM on their projects and career goals.
  - Stakeholder mapping: meet with Eng manager, Data lead, Marketing lead, Sales/CS reps, and key partners.
  - Audit metrics: review dashboard for acquisition, activation, retention, conversion funnels, LTV/CAC; read recent experiment results and postmortems.
  - Read current roadmap, OKRs, and backlog; attend key rituals (standups, sprint planning, retros).
- Deliverables / success signals:
  - Written summary of current state: top 3 growth levers, active experiments, technical constraints, and team skill gaps.
  - Shared initial priorities and questions with your manager and key stakeholders.
  - Established 1:1 cadences with PMs and stakeholders.

60-day goals — Stabilize & deliver
- Objectives:
  - Start delivering on a prioritized bet or experiment; reduce friction in cross-functional workflow.
  - Define decision-making framework for prioritization and resource allocation.
- Key activities:
  - Prioritize top 2–3 growth experiments/initiatives and own kickoff with clear hypotheses and metrics.
  - Implement or refine weekly growth sync (cross-functional experimental review) and a roadmap prioritization cadence.
  - Introduce a template for experiments (hypothesis, success metrics, sample size, rollout plan).
  - Begin mentoring sessions (e.g., weekly coaching topics) with each PM; shadow their stakeholder meetings where helpful.
- Deliverables / success signals:
  - At least 1 experiment launched with measurable success criteria.
  - A documented prioritization framework (e.g., ICE/PIE + effort estimate) adopted by the squad.
  - Reduction in cross-team blockers or faster decision times.

90-day goals — Scale & lead
- Objectives:
  - Demonstrate measurable growth impact, scale repeatable processes, and prepare the team for longer-term roadmap execution.
- Key activities:
  - Analyze experiment results, iterate on winning ideas, and decide scale vs kill.
  - Set or refine growth OKRs for the next quarter with clear owner accountability.
  - Formalize mentoring/career development plan for the PMs (growth goals, skill development).
  - Introduce a quarterly planning/retrospective ritual that ties experiments to OKRs.
- Deliverables / success signals:
  - Documented wins with impact metrics (e.g., % increase in activation/conversion or experiments moving MQL→SQL).
  - Growth playbook: prioritized experiments, decision criteria, and rollout playbooks.
  - PMs demonstrating increased ownership (leading experiments end-to-end).

Example weekly cadence (first 90 days)
- 1:1s: weekly 30–45 min with each PM (focus first 30 days on listening, then coaching & blockers).
- Growth squad sync: weekly 30–60 min for status on experiments, metrics, and blockers.
- Cross-functional growth review: weekly/biweekly 45 min with Data, Eng, Marketing to review learnings and prioritize next experiments.
- Roadmap/Strategy check-in: biweekly with manager and Eng lead.
- Office hours: 1 hour/week for anyone across company to propose growth ideas.

Balancing hands-on work vs leadership — practical guidance
- Time split suggestion (initial ramp):
  - First month: 60% hands-on (learn, audits, run initial experiments), 40% leadership (1:1s, stakeholder alignment).
  - Months 2–3: shift to ~40% hands-on, 60% leadership/strategy/mentorship.
  - Long term: target ~20–30% hands-on, 70–80% leadership (delegate execution while owning strategy and decision-making).
- Tactics to maintain impact while leading:
  - Delegate with clarity: when assigning experiments, define hypothesis, success metrics, owner, timeline, and decision gate up front.
  - Create reusable templates and playbooks so PMs can run experiments consistently without you in the weeds.
  - Time block your calendar: reserve deep-work blocks for strategy and separate slots for 1:1s and syncs.
  - “Teach, don’t do”: in 1:1s, ask questions to guide decisions rather than taking over; have PMs present options and recommended actions.
  - Office hours and weekly reviews: provides a consistent place for hands-on feedback without daily firefighting.
  - Use metrics and dashboards as your “ears”: if you can trust the numbers and experiment reports, you’ll need fewer status checks.

Quick tips for mentoring 3 PMs
- Start with their career goals and strengths; co-create a 90-day development plan for each.
- Use a coaching model: Situation → Options → Recommendation and ask them to propose solutions before you decide.
- Pair on 1–2 key decisions initially; transition to review/approve model with clear decision rights.
- Provide regular feedback (positive + one growth area) and celebrate wins publicly.

KPIs and metrics to prioritize for Growth
- Acquisition: conversion rate from UA channels, CAC by channel, new users per channel
- Activation: % users completing the A-ha / activation milestone
- Retention: day 7/30 retention, cohort retention curves
- Monetization: trial-to-paid conversion, ARPU, LTV

KPIs to track (definitions + what to watch)
- Activation
  - Definition: % of new users who complete the “activation event” (your product’s A‑ha moment) within X days of signup.
  - How to measure: funnel: signup → activation event; track conversion rate and time‑to‑activation distribution.
  - Signal to act: an experiment that moves activation by a relative +5–10% (or improves time‑to‑activation materially) is meaningful; exact threshold should match your baseline and traffic.

- Retention
  - Definition: cohort retention measured at D7 and D30 (users who return / perform a key action).
  - How to measure: cohort curves by acquisition date; rolling retention metrics.
  - Signal to act: changes in D7/D30 of 2–5% (absolute) are often meaningful; also watch shape of curve (improved long‑term engagement is better than short spikes).

- Conversion
  - Definition: signup → paid (or trial → paid) conversion %; also consider conversion at other funnel stages (activation→paid).
  - How to measure: funnel conversion rate, time to convert, conversion by channel.
  - Signal to act: look for relative improvements vs. baseline; experiments that materially reduce time‑to‑pay or increase conversion by a few percent can move revenue.

I’m excited to share that I’ve been promoted to Senior Product Manager at [Company]! Deep thanks to my manager, mentors, and the amazing cross-functional team who make our work possible — your partnership, feedback, and hustle are everything. 30/60/90 plan — punchy, outcome-focused

Overall goals: build credibility, uncover immediate impact areas (quick wins), transfer tactical work through delegation, and build cross-functional trust.

30 days — Listen, map, and score quick wins
- Objective: Understand product, people, processes; achieve 1–2 fast, visible wins.
- Key actions:
  - 1:1s with direct reports (30–45 min), PM peers, Eng leads, Design, Data, Sales/CS, Marketing, and relevant execs. Use a consistent 5-question script (current priorities, biggest risks, what would make your life easier, dependencies, expectations of me).
  - Product audit: metrics, top 10 bugs/incidents, roadmap commitments, backlog health, active experiments.
  - Identify quick wins (see list below) and pick 1–2 to own and finish within 30 days.
  - Clarify roles & decision rights for current projects (RACI for top 3 initiatives).
- Success metrics:
  - Completed 90% of scheduled 1:1s.
  - Deliver 1 quick win with measurable improvement (e.g., decrease support tickets by X%, reduce load time by Y%).
  - Roadmap/priority document shared with stakeholders.
- Delegation & process:
  - Start delegating 2–3 tactical tasks (e.g., backlog grooming, experiment setup) to PMs/Owners with clear success criteria and deadlines.
  - One weekly 15–30m check-in with delegates.

60 days — Align, strengthen team, and hand off tactical work
- Objective: Drive medium-impact delivery and institutionalize delegation.
- Key actions:
  - Propose a prioritized 6–12 week short roadmap of experiments/features tied to outcomes.
  - Coach direct reports on trade-off decisions; run a joint planning session to align on priorities.
  - Implement or refine lightweight delivery cadences (weekly standup, biweekly roadmap sync, monthly metrics review).
  - Start handing off ownership of recurring tactical work to PMs and define escalation paths.
- Success metrics:
  - At least 2 initiatives in active delivery with clear KPIs.
  - Delegated tasks moved to owners with status showing progress; you’re spending <50% time on execution.
  - Stakeholder satisfaction (quick pulse) showing clearer alignment.
- Delegation & process:
  - Use clear templates: outcome, success metrics, timeline, risks, decision authority.
  - Empower one PM to be your “deputy” for day-to-day issues.

90 days — Deliver measurable outcomes and scale
- Objective: Demonstrate impact, refine strategy, and scale your team’s autonomy.
- Key actions:
  - Ship one medium-impact feature or run a validated experiment and present results with learnings.
  - Formalize a 6–12 month product strategy (vision, themes, metrics) informed by earlier findings.
  - Optimize org processes—handbook page for onboarding new product work, playbooks for prioritization and experiments.
  - Coach and provide career feedback to direct reports; identify skill gaps.
- Success metrics:
  - Targeted KPI improvements (e.g., activation +10%, churn -5%, support tickets -30% — pick what matters).
  - Team is running delivery independently; you’re in a strategic & coaching role 60–75% of the time.
  - A documented roadmap and stakeholder-aligned plan for next quarter.

Quick-win ideas (pick 1–2 in first 30 days)
- Analytics clarity: fix or add a key event that was missing so you can measure a critical funnel drop-off (impact: immediate insight).
- Backlog triage: remove or reprioritize 20–30% of low-value tickets; reduce triage time.
- UX tidy: ship a small copy or layout fix causing frequent support tickets.
- Priority unblock: resolve top three blockers in the delivery pipeline (e.g., address a blocker in CI/CD or data access).
- Customer insight: run five customer calls focused on a high-impact problem and synthesize findings for engineering/design.

Delegation playbook — quick practical rules
- Delegate outcomes, not tasks: define the “what” and the success metric; let people own the “how.”
- Match authority to responsibility: explicitly state decision boundaries and who to escalate to.
- Use short cadences: 15–30m weekly updates + shared dashboard; avoid micromanagement.
- Teach, don’t rescue: ask guiding questions and review proposals rather than doing the work.
- Feedback loop: after completion, do a short retro with the owner—what worked, what didn’t.

Relationship-building checklist
- First 30 days: schedule 1:1s (directs + key partners), listen, document commitments.
- Stakeholder map: who makes decisions, who influences, what they care about.
- Quick credibility moves: deliver one committed quick win and present outcomes.
- Ongoing: run a monthly stakeholder demo/metrics sync and quarterly roadmap alignment.

Fantastic — congrats again. Below is a practical, tangible 30/60/90-day plan focused on your three core responsibilities: owning the roadmap, aligning cross-functional stakeholders, and mentoring junior PMs. Pick or adapt the actions and deliverables to your org’s cadence and priorities.

High-level approach
- 30 days = Learn, diagnose, and build credibility.
- 60 days = Plan, align stakeholders, and start executing.
- 90 days = Deliver early wins, iterate, and ramp mentoring/ownership.

30 days — Learn & diagnose (observe, build context, quick wins)
- Objectives
  - Understand product, customers, KPIs, tech constraints, and team dynamics.
  - Build relationships and credibility with engineers, design, sales, CS, marketing, analytics, and execs.
  - Identify the top 2–3 opportunities/risks to address in the next 60–90 days.
- Actions
  - Read product docs, roadmap history, recent retros, OKRs, analytics dashboards.
  - Meet 1:1 with your manager, each direct report, product stakeholders, and key partners (30–60 minute intro + discovery).
  - Shadow customer calls / support tickets / sales demos for direct customer context.
  - Review backlog, active sprints, and release cadence; assess technical debt and blocking issues.
  - Run a quick stakeholder mapping exercise (who influences, who decides, who needs buy-in).
- Deliverables (end of 30 days)
  - 1-page product summary + current metrics and top 3 risks/opportunities.
  - Stakeholder map and recommended communication cadence.
  - Draft 30/60/90 objectives shared with your manager for alignment.
- Success metrics
  - Completed 1:1s with key stakeholders (target: 15–20).
  - Clear list of 3 prioritized opportunities with evidence.

60 days — Plan & align (create a coherent roadmap and secure buy-in)
- Objectives
  - Create a prioritized roadmap aligned to business goals.
  - Get cross-functional commitment on scope, timeline, and success metrics.
  - Begin mentoring rhythm with junior PMs and assign clear learning goals.
- Actions
  - Run a roadmap prioritization session (use RICE, effort vs impact, OKR alignment).
  - Host a cross-functional roadmap review workshop to surface dependencies and risks.
  - Finalize quarterly OKRs/metrics tied to roadmap items.
  - Set recurring cadences: roadmap sync, release review, weekly PM standup.
  - Start regular 1:1s with junior PMs, do pairing sessions on discovery and prioritization.
- Deliverables (end of 60 days)
  - A 90-day product roadmap with priorities, owners, high-level timelines, and success metrics.
  - Risk & dependency register and mitigation plan.
  - Mentorship plans for each junior PM (goals, skill gaps, paired projects).
- Success metrics
  - Stakeholder sign-off on roadmap (documented feedback and agreement).
  - Mentorship program established (1:1 cadence set, initial goals documented).

90 days — Deliver & scale (ship momentum and embed processes)
- Objectives
  - Deliver first measurable outcomes from roadmap work.
  - Demonstrate cross-functional alignment and predictable delivery.
  - Show growth in junior PMs' autonomy and capability.
- Actions
  - Execute on first prioritized initiative(s) and measure results against success metrics.
  - Run a post-release review and iterate quickly on user feedback and metrics.
  - Implement improvements to delivery process (planning, estimations, retros).
  - Formalize career and development plans for junior PMs (training, shadowing, stretch goals).
- Deliverables (end of 90 days)
  - Delivered feature/initiative with outcome metrics report.
  - Team-retrospective and updated roadmap for the next quarter.
  - Progress report to manager/execs: wins, learnings, next risks.
- Success metrics
  - Delivery predictability (X% of committed features released on time).
  - Stakeholder satisfaction (survey or qualitative feedback improved).
  - Measurable progress on at least one junior PM skill (e.g., independent discovery, stakeholder facilitation).

Meeting & cadence templates (quick)
- Stakeholder map: list name, role, influence level, preferred communication, top concern, required approvals.
- Roadmap sync cadence: monthly executive sync (30–60m), biweekly product triage (30m), weekly PM/eng sync (30m).
- 1:1 agenda for junior PMs: wins, blockers, learning topic, project decisions, career check-in (30–45m).

Prioritization criteria examples
- Business impact (revenue, retention, activation)
- Customer value (frequency/severity of request)
- Strategic alignment (OKRs)
- Effort & complexity (engineering, legal, data)
- Risk reduction (security/technical debt)

Mentoring checklist (first 90 days)
- Week 1–4: shadow their meetings, review discovery docs, give feedback on prioritization.
- Week 5–8: pair on roadmap decisions, co-lead a cross-functional meeting.
- Week 9–12: delegate ownership of a small initiative with you as safety net; run a feedback session post-release.

Common risks & mitigations
- Risk: Stakeholder misalignment — Mitigate: early workshops, clear success metrics, documented agreements.
- Risk: Overcommitting — Mitigate: reduce scope, timebox experiments, separate discovery vs delivery.
- Risk: Junior PMs feel unsupported — Mitigate: set clear goals, weekly coaching, public recognition for wins.

I picked sensible defaults so you can copy/paste immediately; if you want I’ll swap in your real product name, exec names, start date, or timezone.

Placeholders I used

- Execs / stakeholders: Sarah Chen (CEO), Mark Rivera (CFO), Anil Patel (CTO), Jessica Lee (VP Sales), Maria Gomez (Head of Data)

1) Calendar invite texts (copy into Google/Outlook calendar)
Note: I used a Monday start for Week 1. Replace [DATE] with the actual dates, and add Zoom/meeting links as needed.

Week 1 — Orientation & relationship building
- Event: Kickoff — 1:1 with Manager (Expectations & Q3 priorities)
  - When: Week 1, Day 1 — 09:00–09:30
  - Attendees: You, [Manager]
  - Agenda: role expectations, success metrics, communication cadence, top Q3 asks, immediate blockers.
  - Location: Zoom / Office

- Event: Team intro & alignment (All PMs + Eng leads)
  - When: Week 1, Day 1 — 10:00–11:30
  - Attendees: 6 PMs, Eng Manager(s), Design lead
  - Agenda: quick intros, your role & priorities, current sprint context, immediate support needs.

- Event: 1:1s — PMs (x6)
  - When: Week 1, Days 2–3 — 30 min each (stagger throughout)
  - Attendees: You + each PM
  - Agenda: current ownership, top blockers, discovery status, career goals.

- Event: 1:1s — Eng leads, Design, Data, Sales, CS, Marketing
  - When: Week 1, Days 3–5 — 30–45 min each
  - Attendees: You + each function lead
  - Agenda: tech constraints, capacity, KPI ownership, enterprise asks, support escalations.

- Event: Customer call shadowing

  - When: Week 4, Day 3 — 14:00–15:00

- Weekly PM + Eng sync — Tue 09:00–09:30
- Biweekly cross-functional roadmap — Wed 11:00–12:00 (every other week)
- Monthly exec roadmap & KPI review — First Thursday 10:30–11:00

2) Exec slide deck (1–2 slides) — slide text + speaker notes
Slide 1 — Title slide / 30‑day summary
- Title: PulseAnalytics — 30‑day update & asks (Q3 launch)
- Bullets:
  - Role: Senior Product Manager (roadmap, alignment, mentoring) — 30 days in role
  - Immediate focus: finalize roadmap + KPIs for Q3 launch (10 weeks)
  - Key accomplishments: 1:1s with PMs/Eng/Design/Data/Sales/CS; drafted 90‑day roadmap; KPI spec prototype; stakeholder map & risk register
- Speaker notes (30–60s): Quick personal intro, emphasize momentum and team alignment. Summarize that we completed discovery and are ready to make scope decisions for Q3.

Slide 2 — Roadmap snapshot, KPIs & asks
- Header: Q3 priorities (top 3), owner, timeline
  - 1) Stabilize KPI sources (Data pipeline fixes) — Owner: Maria Gomez — Timeline: Weeks 1–4 (high priority)
  - 2) Lightweight analytics view (Plan A for Q3) — Owner: [PM name] — Timeline: Weeks 3–9
  - 3) Dashboard UX improvements (high adoption uplift) — Owner: [PM name] — Timeline: Weeks 4–12
- KPIs (targets for Q3 launch)
  - Activation (first 7-day feature usage): +15% (target)
  - Key enterprise metric accuracy (error rate): <2% within pipeline
  - Adoption (top-50 accounts usage of new view): 30% within first 30 days
- Top risks & mitigation asks
  - Risk: Data pipeline gaps — Ask: 2-sprint priority for Data Eng to stabilize sources.
  - Risk: Integration dependencies — Ask: exec signoff to narrow scope to “lightweight” variant as Plan A.
- Speaker notes (60–90s): Run through priorities, tie each item to a KPI, and clearly state the two asks: (1) exec approval to prioritize the lightweight launch as Plan A, (2) temporary Data Eng capacity for pipeline stabilization.

I can convert this into a PPT/Google Slides file and include the speaker notes if you’d like the actual slide deck file.

3) RICE scoring sheet (sample population)
Formula used: RICE = (Reach * Impact * Confidence) / Effort
(Reach = number of customers/users impacted in the quarter; Impact = 1–5 scale where 5 = major; Confidence = 0–1; Effort = person-weeks)

Columns: Initiative | Reach | Impact (1–5) | Confidence (0–1) | Effort (person-weeks) | RICE score | Notes

Sample rows:
1) Data pipeline stabilization (KPI source fixes)
- Reach: 300
- Impact: 4
- Confidence: 0.90
- Effort: 10
- RICE = (300*4*0.9)/10 = 108
- Notes: Improves metric accuracy for enterprise customers; prerequisite for reliable KPIs.

2) Lightweight analytics view (Plan A for Q3)
- Reach: 250
- Impact: 4
- Confidence: 0.80
- Effort: 8
- RICE = (250*4*0.8)/8 = 100
- Notes: Reduced-scope feature expected to deliver quick adoption with lower engineering cost.

3) Dashboard UX revamp (high-frequency users)
- Reach: 400
- Impact: 3
- Confidence: 0.70
- Effort: 12
- RICE = (400*3*0.7)/12 = 70
- Notes: Broad usage impact; medium effort.

4) Self-service report builder (longer term)
- Reach: 150
- Impact: 4
- Confidence: 0.50
- Effort: 24
- RICE = (150*4*0.5)/24 = 12.5
- Notes: High effort, lower confidence for Q3.

5) Enterprise integrations (SSO + data connectors)
- Reach: 60
- Impact: 5
- Confidence: 0.60
- Effort: 20
- RICE = (60*5*0.6)/20 = 9
- Notes: High impact for new enterprise deals but high effort and longer lead.

Ranked by RICE score (highest → lowest)
1. Data pipeline stabilization — 108
2. Lightweight analytics view — 100
3. Dashboard UX revamp — 70
4. Self‑service report builder — 12.5
5. Enterprise integrations — 9

How to use this: use the RICE scores as a data point in your prioritization workshop; adjust Reach/Impact/Confidence with input from Sales, CS, and Data to reflect enterprise account weight and risk tolerance. If execs require enterprise features for deals, weight Impact higher or treat some work as non-negotiable (i.e., not purely prioritized by RICE).

4) Next steps / how I can finalize these artifacts for you
- Swap placeholder names/product: tell me the product name and exact exec/stakeholder names and I’ll update the slides, email, and invite attendee lists.
- Generate calendar invites (ICS) or directly populate Google Calendar: tell me the start date and your timezone and I’ll create ICS files or provide one-click Google Calendar event links.
- Create the actual slide deck file (PPTX or Google Slides) and/or the RICE sheet as a Google Sheet I can share.
- Tailor the RICE sheet with real Reach numbers from your analytics tool — I can help pull/estimate those if you provide shared metrics.

Which of the above would you like me to do next? If you want the calendar invites or slide deck files now, tell me the start date and timezone and confirm the exec names (or provide replacements) and I’ll generate the files.

- Plan for delegation and team development so you can focus on higher‑level work.

messages.speaker: responder_agent
messages.content:
Fantastic — congrats again. Below is a tailored 30‑60‑90 plan for a Senior Product Manager owning cross‑functional roadmaps and a team of five, plus a prioritized list of high‑impact questions to ask your manager. Use this as a working template you can adapt to your org’s specifics.

30‑60‑90 plan (objectives, actions, deliverables, success metrics)

First 30 days — Learn, build relationships, and assess
- Objective: Rapidly get up to speed on product, team, stakeholders, and metrics so you can diagnose opportunity areas and earn trust.
- Key actions
  - One‑on‑ones with each direct report (focus: strengths, blockers, career goals, recent wins).
  - Meet key stakeholders: engineering lead(s), design, marketing, sales, customer success, analytics, finance, support, legal, and any cross‑functional partners.
  - Meet your manager to confirm priorities and immediate expectations (use the questions below).
  - Audit current roadmap, product strategy, OKRs, and backlog; review product analytics, usage funnels, NPS/CSAT, SLAs, revenue & churn data.
  - Sit in customer calls / review top support tickets and major customer feedback.
  - Observe team rituals (planning, standups, demos, retros) and delivery cadence.
  - Identify 1–2 low‑effort, high‑impact quick wins.
- Deliverables (end of 30 days)
  - Stakeholder map with communication cadence.
  - Annotated roadmap: what’s committed, what’s ambiguous, key dependencies and risks.
  - Team skills/role gap summary and individual development notes.
  - Short list of 1–2 recommended quick wins and rationale.
- Success metrics / signals
  - Completed one‑on‑ones with all directs and primary stakeholders.
  - Clear understanding of top 5 product KPIs and baseline numbers.
  - Agreement with manager on top 3 priorities for your role.

Days 31–60 — Align, plan, and start implementing
- Objective: Build alignment across stakeholders, refine the roadmap, launch quick wins, and improve processes to increase predictability.
- Key actions
  - Share findings and proposed roadmap adjustments with manager and core stakeholders; get buy‑in.
  - Prioritize backlog using a clear framework (e.g., value / effort, OKR alignment).
  - Run a cross‑functional roadmap workshop to align on themes, timelines, and dependencies.
  - Implement one quick win (MVP) with your team; measure impact.
  - Introduce or refine team processes (e.g., definition of done, planning cadence, OKR check‑ins, customer feedback loops).
  - Begin addressing team development gaps (training, pairing, hiring plan).
- Deliverables (end of 60 days)
  - A revised 90‑day roadmap with milestones, owners, and dependencies.
  - Post‑launch report for the quick win: metrics, learnings, next steps.
  - Process improvements rolled out (e.g., weekly roadmap sync, clearer PRD template).
  - Hiring / role plan if gaps identified.
- Success metrics / signals
  - Stakeholder alignment on the revised roadmap.
  - Measurable improvement from quick‑win (engagement uplift, reduced friction, etc.).
  - Improved predictability in sprint/feature delivery.

Days 61–90 — Execute, measure impact, and scale
- Objective: Deliver measurable outcomes, lock in processes, and set longer‑term strategy and team growth plans.
- Key actions
  - Execute higher‑impact roadmap items and coordinate cross‑functional launches.
  - Establish a regular product review cadence (monthly product metrics review, quarterly roadmap review).
  - Formalize team development plans and career ladders; start recruiting if needed.
  - Introduce experiments and A/B testing for key hypotheses.
  - Prepare 90‑day presentation for manager and stakeholders with outcomes, learnings, and recommendations for next quarter.
- Deliverables (end of 90 days)
  - Measured outcomes for launched initiatives (KPIs vs baseline).
  - Roadmap & OKRs for next quarter aligned to business goals.
  - Team development plan and any hiring requisitions.
  - Retrospective summary: what worked, what didn’t, and improvement actions.
- Success metrics / signals
  - Demonstrable KPI improvements tied to your initiatives.
  - Cross‑functional alignment and clearer decisioning process.
  - Positive feedback from manager, peers, and team on progress and leadership.

Practical rituals & cadence to set up early
- Weekly: 1:1s with directs (30–60 min), engineering lead sync, roadmap sync.
- Biweekly: Sprint planning / review / retro cadence alignment with team.
- Monthly: Product metrics review with stakeholders, customer insights review.
- Quarterly: Roadmap and OKR planning + cross‑org stakeholder review.

Suggested KPIs to track (pick top 3–5 relevant to your product)
- Adoption: new users, activation rate, feature adoption %
- Engagement: DAU/MAU or session length, stickiness
- Retention/churn: 7/30/90‑day retention, churn rate
- Revenue/monetization: MRR/ARR, ARPU, conversion rate
- Operational: cycle time, mean time to resolve customer issues, % of roadmap delivered on time
- Quality & satisfaction: NPS, CSAT, bug escape rate

High‑impact questions to ask your manager (grouped and prioritized)
- Expectations & success criteria
  - What does “success” look like for me at 30/60/90 days and at 6 months? (clarifies short and medium expectations)
  - Which business metrics or OKRs am I explicitly accountable for? (ties your work to measurable outcomes)
- Strategy & priorities
  - What are the top strategic priorities for the product this year? Which can/should I deprioritize? (helps with trade‑offs)
  - Are there corporate initiatives or exec expectations that must be reflected on our roadmap? (exposes hidden constraints)
- Roadmap & decision rights
  - Who has final say on roadmap trade‑offs? What’s the decision process for conflicts between teams? (clarifies governance)
  - How much autonomy do I have to reallocate roadmap items or propose new bets? (determines your authority)
- Stakeholders & dependencies
  - Who are the influential stakeholders I should get buy‑in from first? Any historical tensions I should know about? (maps political landscape)
  - Which teams do we consistently rely on (e.g., infra, data, sales), and are there SLA or resource constraints? (surface blockers)
- Customers & market
  - Which customer segments matter most to our strategy, and who are our top customers to engage for feedback? (prioritizes research)
  - Are there known competitive threats or upcoming market shifts I should prioritize? (context)
- Resources & constraints
  - What budget, headcount, and external resources are available to me? Are there hiring plans I should align with? (practical limitations)
  - Any technical debt, compliance, or platform work on the horizon that will consume capacity? (hidden work)
- Team & hiring
  - Do you see any immediate team structure changes or roles we should hire for? How should I approach performance reviews and promotions? (people strategy)
  - What are your expectations for how I’ll develop and mentor this team? (management style)
- Communication & feedback
  - How often would you like status updates and in what format? (email, dash, recap meeting)
  - What’s your preferred way to receive escalations and solve disagreements? (communication norms)
- Risk & escalation
  - What are the biggest risks you see for this product or org right now, and how should I escalate issues? (risk posture)
  - If I face a strategic disagreement with another leader, what approach should I take? (escalation path)
- Personal development
  - What growth opportunities should I focus on this year as a Senior PM? (career guidance)
  - Is there anyone you recommend I shadow or learn from in the org? (mentorship)

Quick scripts & tips
- 1:1 kickoff with direct reports: “I want to support your goals and remove blockers. Tell me what’s going well, what’s holding you back, and where you want to grow.”
- Roadmap workshop kickoff: present current state, hypothesize top outcomes, run a collaborative priority exercise (impact vs effort), and capture decisions and owners.
- Quick‑win pitch to manager: brief problem statement, proposed experiment, required resources, expected impact, and how you’ll measure success.

If you’d like, I can:
- Turn this into a slide‑ready 30‑60‑90 presentation,
- Draft the email/agenda for your first all‑hands or roadmap workshop,
- Create a one‑page stakeholder map template you can copy.

Which of those would be most helpful next?

- Slide 12 — Thank you / Q&A / Contact
  - Content: “Questions, feedback, next steps”

  - Speaker note: Ask for immediate scheduling of follow‑ups and stakeholder 1:1s.

Workshop agenda + materials
- Duration: 90–120 minutes recommended (I suggest 2 hours if many stakeholders)
- Attendees: Engineering leads, Design lead, Analytics, Marketing/GTM, Sales/CS rep, QA, Product Ops, PM team (you), any exec sponsor

Suggested 2‑hour agenda (timeboxed)

- 10–20 min — Quick product & business context (you/manager) — Outcome: shared north star & success metrics
- 20–35 min — Current roadmap + major themes (you) — Outcome: clarity on commitments & open questions
- 35–60 min — Prioritization exercise (impact vs effort) — Activity: small groups or everyone votes on candidate initiatives — Outcome: prioritized list
- 60–80 min — Dependency & risk mapping — Activity: map owners/constraints and surface blockers — Outcome: mitigation plan & owners
- 80–95 min — Decide next steps & owners for top initiatives — Outcome: owners, timelines, success metrics
- 95–105 min — Communications & cadence agreements (syncs, reporting) — Outcome: agree on regular touchpoints

First 30 days — Learn & Build Trust (May 15–June 14)
Objective: Get context, build relationships, and discover immediate opportunities related to onboarding, releases, and churn.
Key actions

- Review artifacts: product roadmap, specs for onboarding feature, release notes/history (past 6 months), CI/CD pipeline docs, customer churn reports, NPS/CSAT trends, support tickets data, and analytics dashboards.
- Do a quick audit of the current release process: cycle time, rollback frequency, and deployment pain points.
- Do a churn triage: segment churn (time-to-churn, cohorts, reasons) and identify top 3 drivers.
- Identify 1–2 quick wins: e.g., small onboarding copy/UI tweak that increases activation, a lightweight release checklist to reduce last-minute rollbacks, or a churn-trigger email sequence.

- 100% of direct reports and key stakeholders met.
- Documented list: top 5 risks/opportunities for onboarding, release cadence, and churn.

Days 31–60 — Plan & Pilot (June 15–July 14)
Objective: Create a validated launch plan for onboarding, pilot release cadence improvements, and run initial churn-reduction experiments.
Key actions
- Finalize onboarding MVP scope and launch plan (acceptance criteria, telemetry, rollout strategy, success metrics).
- Work with engineering/DevOps to create a concrete release cadence plan (e.g., biweekly sprints with a predictable release day or a weekly release window). Pilot a change with a single service or small set of changes.
- Design 2–3 retention experiments for top churn drivers (in-product prompts, onboarding follow-up flows, targeted outreach by CS).
- Set up dashboards: activation (time-to-first-value), onboarding completion rate, release frequency/lead time, rollback rate, and monthly churn rate by cohort.
- Run a backlog grooming session and clarify ownership/SLAs for release activities.
- Host a team workshop to align on goals, definition of “done,” and ways of working for releases and feature rollouts.

Success measures
- Approved onboarding launch plan with dates and owners.
- Pilot release cadence executed with measurable reduction in lead time or rollback incidents.
- At least one churn experiment running with baseline metrics established.

Days 61–90 — Execute & Scale (July 15–Aug 14)
Objective: Launch the onboarding feature, embed an improved release cadence, and show measurable churn reduction signals.
Key actions
- Launch onboarding MVP with phased roll-out (feature flags, pilot cohort) and monitor activation/retention in real time. Run A/B tests where useful.
- Operationalize the new release cadence (release playbook, checklist, postmortem process). Make it standard operating procedure.
- Evaluate churn experiment results, double down on the winning tactics, and turn successful experiments into product changes or CS workflows.
- Present a 90-day review to leadership and stakeholders: wins, metrics, learnings, and recommended priorities for the next quarter (hiring, investments, larger roadmap items).
- Identify talent/development needs on the team and propose training or hiring if gaps are blocking the roadmap.

Success measures
- Onboarding feature launched to target cohort with improvement in activation/time-to-first-value vs baseline.
- Release cadence metrics: increased release frequency and decreased mean time to deploy/rollback rate.
- Early churn metrics show improvement (reduction in short-term churn or improved retention in target cohort).

Suggested success metrics (pick 3–5 to track)
- Activation rate / time-to-first-value (for onboarding)
- % of users completing onboarding flow
- Release frequency (releases/month) and mean lead time for changes
- Rollback or incident rate per release
- Monthly churn rate by cohort and 30/60-day retention
- NPS or CSAT for newly onboarded users

Operational cadence & communication
- Weekly: Product + Eng sync (status, blockers), team standup
- Biweekly: Roadmap/release planning
- Monthly: Stakeholder update (one-pager: Objective, Progress, Blockers, Next steps)
- Post-release: Short writeup with metrics & learnings

messages.content:
Congrats again—that’s a huge step. Below I’ve put together a focused, practical 30/60/90-day plan tailored for a new Senior Product Manager who’s leading a small team and owning the roadmap, plus two punchy LinkedIn announcement options (short and longer) you can use or adapt.

30/60/90-day plan (objectives, actions, and success measures)

Guiding principles
- Lead with listening and alignment in Month 1, then set direction and quick wins in Month 2, and scale impact and processes in Month 3.
- Balance people, product, and stakeholder work: build trust with your team, understand the product and customers, and set a roadmap that delivers measurable value.

Days 0–30: Understand, build trust, and assess
Primary objective: Get grounded—team dynamics, product state, customers, and key stakeholders.

Key actions
- Introductions & relationships
  - 1:1s with each direct report (weekly thereafter) to learn motivations, blockers, career goals.
  - 1:1s with key stakeholders: engineering lead, design lead, sales, CS, marketing, analytics, legal.
  - Skip-level meetings (if applicable) to understand broader context.
- Product & data audit
  - Review current roadmap, backlog, OKRs, KPIs, metrics dashboards, recent release notes.
  - Run a basic health check: technical debt, churn drivers, key bugs, blocked epics.
- Customer & market discovery
  - Sit in support calls, review top customer feedback and NPS, meet 3–5 customers or partners.
- Team & process observation
  - Observe planning, grooming, stand-ups, retro—note strengths and friction.
- Deliverables
  - 1-page “Current State” summary (strengths, risks, top 3 opportunities).
  - Draft list of short-term quick wins and dependencies.

Success measures (how you’ll know Month 1 worked)
- Completed 1:1s with all direct reports and all major stakeholders.
- Clear product health dashboard pulled together.
- Shared Current State summary with leadership and team, with feedback incorporated.

Days 31–60: Align, prioritize, and deliver quick wins
Primary objective: Set prioritized roadmap direction, deliver early value, and align stakeholders.

Key actions
- Strategy & prioritization
  - Run a prioritization workshop (RICE, MoSCoW, or PIRATE as suits org) with stakeholders.
  - Define or refine success metrics for top initiatives.
- Launch quick wins
  - Execute 1–2 tactical improvements from Month 1 (e.g., reduce activation friction, fix top bugs, small UX refinements).
- Roadmap & communication
  - Present proposed 90–180 day roadmap to leadership, including trade-offs and expected impact.
  - Establish regular roadmap cadence and shared repository (Confluence, Notion).
- Team enablement
  - Define working agreements, sprint cadence, definition of done, and clear ownership for epics.
  - Start career development plans for direct reports (next steps + expectations).
- Deliverables
  - Prioritized backlog and a validated 90-day roadmap.
  - Post-mortem/metrics on quick win outcomes.

Success measures
- At least one quick win launched with measurable impact (improved conversion, reduced bugs, positive customer feedback).
- Stakeholder alignment on priorities and clear decision log.
- Team feels clearer on responsibilities and cadence (survey or quick check-in).

Days 61–90: Execute, measure, and scale
Primary objective: Drive toward measurable outcomes, refine processes, and set longer-term strategy.

Key actions
- Execution & measurement
  - Track outcomes against the success metrics for roadmap initiatives.
  - Run experiments where possible and document learnings.
- Process improvements
  - Implement any needed changes to delivery predictability (e.g., capacity planning, better sprint planning).
  - Introduce product KPIs dashboard with alerts and weekly reporting.
- People & growth
  - Conduct mid-quarter 1:1s to review progress and adjust development plans.
  - Identify hiring needs or upskilling for team capacity.
- Strategy & long-term vision
  - Draft 6–12 month product strategy aligned to company goals; present to leadership for buy-in.
- Deliverables
  - 90-day retrospective with outcomes vs. goals.
  - 6–12 month strategy draft and proposed hires/resourcing plan.

Success measures
- Evidence of measurable progress on roadmap KPIs (examples: +X% activation, -Y% churn, +Z% feature adoption).
- Clear, repeatable product planning and reporting cadence established.
- Leadership and team buy-in to the strategic direction.

Suggested metrics you might track
- Adoption & activation rates, DAU/MAU (if consumer/SaaS), conversion funnel metrics
- Retention/churn, NPS or CSAT changes
- Time-to-market and cycle time for features
- Delivery predictability (commit-to-delivery rate)
- Revenue impact or ARR influenced, if applicable

Quick wins examples (pick 1–3 in first 60 days)
- Fix the top 3 customer-reported UX issues that cause drop-off.
- Optimize onboarding flow to improve activation by X%.
- Stop-gap for a critical bug causing churn.
- A/B test headline or CTA on a high-traffic funnel step.

3) Activation & Churn dashboard layout / template

F. Sample SQL queries (generic — adapt event and table names to your schema)

1) Baseline activation rate (percent achieving key event within 7 days):
-- Assumes events table (event_name, user_id, event_time), users table (user_id, signup_time)
SELECT
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN ke.event_time IS NOT NULL AND ke.event_time <= users.signup_time + INTERVAL '7 day' THEN users.user_id END) AS activated_count,
  COUNT(DISTINCT users.user_id) AS total_signed_up,
  ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN ke.event_time IS NOT NULL AND ke.event_time <= users.signup_time + INTERVAL '7 day' THEN users.user_id END) / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT users.user_id),0),2) AS activation_rate_pct
FROM users
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(event_time) AS event_time
  FROM events
  WHERE event_name = 'key_value_event'
  GROUP BY user_id
) ke ON ke.user_id = users.user_id
WHERE users.signup_time >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 day';

2) Median time-to-activation (in hours) for users who activated:
SELECT
  PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (ke.event_time - users.signup_time))/3600) AS median_hours_to_activation
FROM users
JOIN (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(event_time) AS event_time
  FROM events
  WHERE event_name = 'key_value_event'
  GROUP BY user_id
) ke ON ke.user_id = users.user_id
WHERE ke.event_time IS NOT NULL
  AND users.signup_time >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '90 day';

3) Retention cohort table (weekly cohorts, retained users at 7/30/60 days)
-- This uses signup_week and counts users who had any 'active' event in the window
WITH signups AS (
  SELECT user_id, DATE_TRUNC('week', signup_time)::date AS signup_week
  FROM users
  WHERE signup_time >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '180 day'
),
activity AS (
  SELECT user_id, DATE(event_time) AS activity_date
  FROM events
  WHERE event_name IN ('key_value_event','some_active_event') -- pick events indicating active usage
)
SELECT
  s.signup_week,
  COUNT(DISTINCT s.user_id) AS cohort_size,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN a.activity_date <= s.signup_week + INTERVAL '7 day' THEN s.user_id END) AS retained_7d,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN a.activity_date <= s.signup_week + INTERVAL '30 day' THEN s.user_id END) AS retained_30d,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN a.activity_date <= s.signup_week + INTERVAL '60 day' THEN s.user_id END) AS retained_60d
FROM signups s
LEFT JOIN activity a ON a.user_id = s.user_id
GROUP BY s.signup_week
ORDER BY s.signup_week DESC;

4) Churned accounts in last 30 days (account-level churn)
-- Assumes accounts table with subscription status or events for cancellation
SELECT
  a.account_id,
  a.plan,
  a.revenue_tier,
  a.last_active_at,
  a.cancelled_at,
  a.reason_for_cancel -- if tracked
FROM accounts a
WHERE a.cancelled_at BETWEEN CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 day' AND CURRENT_DATE
ORDER BY a.cancelled_at DESC;

5) Top support ticket reasons for churned accounts
SELECT t.issue_type, COUNT(*) AS count
FROM support_tickets t
JOIN accounts a ON a.account_id = t.account_id
WHERE a.cancelled_at IS NOT NULL
  AND a.cancelled_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '90 day'
GROUP BY t.issue_type
ORDER BY count DESC
LIMIT 10;

6) Simple experiment result (activation conversion by variant)
-- Assumes user->experiment_variant mapping and tracking of activation within window
SELECT
  u.experiment_variant,
  COUNT(DISTINCT u.user_id) AS n_users,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN ke.event_time IS NOT NULL AND ke.event_time <= u.signup_time + INTERVAL '7 day' THEN u.user_id END) AS n_activated,
  ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN ke.event_time IS NOT NULL AND ke.event_time <= u.signup_time + INTERVAL '7 day' THEN u.user_id END) / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT u.user_id),0),2) AS activation_pct
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(event_time) AS event_time
  FROM events
  WHERE event_name = 'key_value_event'
  GROUP BY user_id
) ke ON ke.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE u.experiment_name = 'onboarding_test'
  AND u.signup_time >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '60 day'
GROUP BY u.experiment_variant;

A. BigQuery queries
Notes/assumptions
- events table: events.event_name, events.user_id, events.event_time (TIMESTAMP)
- users table: users.user_id, users.signup_time (TIMESTAMP), users.experiment_name, users.experiment_variant
- accounts table: accounts.account_id, accounts.plan, accounts.revenue_tier, accounts.last_active_at, accounts.cancelled_at, accounts.reason_for_cancel
- support_tickets table: support_tickets.account_id, support_tickets.issue_type

1) Baseline activation rate (percent achieving key_value_event within 7 days)
-- Replace `project.dataset.events` and `project.dataset.users`
WITH first_activation AS (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    MIN(event_time) AS first_event_time
  FROM `project.dataset.events`
  WHERE event_name = 'key_value_event'
  GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT
  COUNTIF(first_event_time IS NOT NULL AND TIMESTAMP_DIFF(first_event_time, u.signup_time, DAY) <= 7) AS activated_count,
  COUNT(DISTINCT u.user_id) AS total_signed_up,
  ROUND(100.0 * COUNTIF(first_event_time IS NOT NULL AND TIMESTAMP_DIFF(first_event_time, u.signup_time, DAY) <= 7) / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT u.user_id),0), 2) AS activation_rate_pct
FROM `project.dataset.users` u
LEFT JOIN first_activation fa
  ON fa.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE u.signup_time >= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 30 DAY);

2) Median time‑to‑activation (hours) for users who activated (approximate)
-- Uses APPROX_QUANTILES to get median
SELECT
  APPROX_QUANTILES(TIMESTAMP_DIFF(fa.first_event_time, u.signup_time, SECOND) / 3600.0, 100)[OFFSET(50)] AS median_hours_to_activation
FROM `project.dataset.users` u
JOIN (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(event_time) AS first_event_time
  FROM `project.dataset.events`
  WHERE event_name = 'key_value_event'
  GROUP BY user_id
) fa
  ON fa.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE u.signup_time >= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 90 DAY);

3) Retention cohort table (weekly sign-up cohorts: retained at 7/30/60 days)
WITH signups AS (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    DATE_TRUNC(DATE(signup_time), WEEK) AS signup_week
  FROM `project.dataset.users`
  WHERE signup_time >= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 180 DAY)
),
first_activity AS (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    MIN(DATE(event_time)) AS first_activity_date
  FROM `project.dataset.events`
  WHERE event_name IN ('key_value_event', 'some_active_event') -- adjust events that signal "active usage"
  GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT
  s.signup_week,
  COUNT(DISTINCT s.user_id) AS cohort_size,
  COUNT(DISTINCT IF(first_activity.first_activity_date IS NOT NULL AND first_activity.first_activity_date <= DATE_ADD(s.signup_week, INTERVAL 7 DAY), s.user_id, NULL)) AS retained_7d,
  COUNT(DISTINCT IF(first_activity.first_activity_date IS NOT NULL AND first_activity.first_activity_date <= DATE_ADD(s.signup_week, INTERVAL 30 DAY), s.user_id, NULL)) AS retained_30d,
  COUNT(DISTINCT IF(first_activity.first_activity_date IS NOT NULL AND first_activity.first_activity_date <= DATE_ADD(s.signup_week, INTERVAL 60 DAY), s.user_id, NULL)) AS retained_60d
FROM signups s
LEFT JOIN first_activity
  ON first_activity.user_id = s.user_id
GROUP BY s.signup_week
ORDER BY s.signup_week DESC;

4) Churned accounts in the last 30 days
SELECT
  a.account_id,
  a.plan,
  a.revenue_tier,
  a.last_active_at,
  a.cancelled_at,
  a.reason_for_cancel
FROM `project.dataset.accounts` a
WHERE a.cancelled_at BETWEEN TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 30 DAY) AND CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()
ORDER BY a.cancelled_at DESC;

5) Top support ticket reasons for churned accounts (last 90 days)
SELECT
  t.issue_type,
  COUNT(*) AS num_tickets
FROM `project.dataset.support_tickets` t
JOIN `project.dataset.accounts` a
  ON a.account_id = t.account_id
WHERE a.cancelled_at IS NOT NULL
  AND a.cancelled_at >= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 90 DAY)
GROUP BY t.issue_type
ORDER BY num_tickets DESC
LIMIT 10;

6) Experiment results: activation conversion by variant (onboarding_test)
WITH first_activation AS (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(event_time) AS first_event_time
  FROM `project.dataset.events`
  WHERE event_name = 'key_value_event'
  GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT
  u.experiment_variant,
  COUNT(DISTINCT u.user_id) AS n_users,
  COUNT(DISTINCT IF(first_activation.first_event_time IS NOT NULL AND TIMESTAMP_DIFF(first_activation.first_event_time, u.signup_time, DAY) <= 7, u.user_id, NULL)) AS n_activated,
  ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT IF(first_activation.first_event_time IS NOT NULL AND TIMESTAMP_DIFF(first_activation.first_event_time, u.signup_time, DAY) <= 7, u.user_id, NULL)) / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT u.user_id),0), 2) AS activation_pct
FROM `project.dataset.users` u
LEFT JOIN first_activation
  ON first_activation.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE u.experiment_name = 'onboarding_test'
  AND u.signup_time >= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 60 DAY)
GROUP BY u.experiment_variant
ORDER BY activation_pct DESC;

If you’d like, I can:
- Convert these into saved views (CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW ...) for your BigQuery project.
- Turn them into Looker explores / LookML or a scheduled Data Studio/Looker dashboard.

30/60/90 plan (focus: quick wins + stakeholder mapping)

30 days — Listen, learn, and score immediate wins

  - Audit existing metrics, projects, and blockers. Identify 2–3 “pain points” you can fix in weeks (process bottlenecks, reporting errors, overdue decisions).
  - Execute a visible quick win (examples below).
  - Document an initial 30/60/90 plan and share with manager for feedback.
- Success metrics (examples)
  - 12 stakeholder meetings completed.
  - 1 quick-win completed and communicated to team.
  - Clear list of top 3 strategic initiatives and top 3 operational risks.

60 days — Build momentum and systems
- Objectives
  - Deepen relationships and begin process improvements.
  - Pilot changes and get stakeholder buy-in.
- Actions
  - Follow-up stakeholder meetings (deeper dives with key influencers).
  - Implement process improvements or new reporting cadence for one area.
  - Start delegating recurring tasks and clarify roles with your team.
  - Launch a small pilot project that addresses an identified pain point.
  - Host a team sync to share vision, quick wins, and near-term goals.
- Success metrics
  - Pilot launched and initial results tracked.
  - Stakeholder satisfaction (qualitative feedback) improved.
  - Clear delegation plan for recurring work.

90 days — Solidify strategy and scale
- Objectives
  - Demonstrate measurable impact and lock in longer-term initiatives.
  - Align on roadmap and KPIs with leadership.
- Actions
  - Review pilot results and iterate or scale successful changes.
  - Present a 6–12 month roadmap (priorities, resource needs, success metrics).
  - Formalize stakeholder engagement plan (regular check-ins, RACI).
  - Establish recurring reporting and performance measures.
- Success metrics
  - Quantified improvement from quick wins/pilot (e.g., % time saved, revenue uplift, reduced cycle time).
  - Stakeholder alignment on top priorities and KPIs.
  - Team clarity on roles and next milestones.

Quick-win ideas (pick 1–2)
- Fix a common reporting error and redistribute accurate report with insights.
- Resolve one long-standing blocker (approval bottleneck, unclear ownership).
- Run a 30-minute “show & tell” demo of something your team already does well to another team—build allies.
- Consolidate duplicate tools/processes to save time (e.g., merge two trackers).

30/60/90 plan — goal: measurably reduce time‑to‑market for feature releases (example target: 20–30% reduction in lead time within 90 days; set exact target after baseline)
  
30 days — baseline, rapid discovery, and a visible quick win
- Objectives
  - Establish baseline metrics and map the current release value stream.
  - Win an early, visible improvement that shows momentum.
  - Begin building alignment with engineering, QA, design, and release stakeholders.
- Key actions
  - Gather metrics: cycle time, lead time (idea → production), commit→deploy time, PR throughput, release frequency, mean time to restore (MTTR), number of hotfixes. If metrics missing, instrument lightweight tracking (sheet or dashboard).
  - Run a value‑stream mapping (1–2 sessions) for a typical feature from discovery → production; identify top 3 bottlenecks (e.g., long code review, flaky tests, manual release steps, unclear acceptance criteria).
  - 1:1s with critical stakeholders: Eng leads, QA lead, Design lead, DevOps/Infra, Release Manager, Product peers, PMs on adjacent squads, Legal/Compliance if needed (20–30 min each). Capture their biggest pain points and improvement ideas.
  - Quick win: pick a high‑impact, low‑effort fix (examples below) and execute it within the month. Communicate outcome widely.
  - Create initial hypothesis list (why releases are slow) and share with manager + team.
- Success metrics (examples)
  - Baseline dashboard in place.
  - 6–8 stakeholder 1:1s completed.
  - 1 quick win executed and communicated (e.g., reduced PR review time by 30% for a sprint).

60 days — pilot changes, streamline processes, and remove blockers
- Objectives
  - Pilot process and tooling changes to shorten key handoffs and automate manual release steps.
  - Reduce variability and increase predictability for one release stream.
- Key actions
  - Launch 1 pilot to address the top bottleneck (examples: introduce feature flags & targeted rollout for risky features; automate slow CI jobs; create a pre‑merged QA environment to parallelize testing).
  - Implement concrete process changes: e.g., defined PR SLAs, short daily release sync for the pilot stream, acceptance criteria templates, branch and merge strategy (trunk based / short‑lived branches).
  - Improve test reliability: identify flaky tests, quarantine or fix them, add test gating for critical paths.
  - Introduce a lightweight release checklist / runbook and a post‑release quick retro for every release in the pilot.
  - Track pilot KPIs weekly and iterate.
- Success metrics
  - Pilot shows measurable improvement (e.g., commit→deploy reduced X%, fewer rollback incidents).
  - Stakeholder feedback positive; adoption plan created to scale changes.

90 days — scale wins, formalize cadence, and set long‑term roadmap
- Objectives
  - Lock in improvements as repeatable processes and scale the successful pilot(s).
  - Present a 6–12 month roadmap to sustain and continue reducing time‑to‑market.
- Key actions
  - Scale successful pilot practices across teams (training, templates, automation).
  - Propose and negotiate a release cadence (e.g., weekly release train or continuous deploy for low‑risk features).
  - Define long‑term investments: expanded CI capacity, end‑to‑end test automation, improved observability, platform improvements.
  - Formalize KPIs and reporting cadence with leadership (monthly report + dashboard).
  - Run a retrospective across teams to codify takeaways and next steps.
- Success metrics
  - Target time‑to‑market reduction achieved (or clear trajectory toward it).
  - Increased release frequency and reduced failure/rollback rate.
  - Roadmap and resource requests approved or queued.

Quick‑win ideas (pick 1–2 in first 30 days)
- Enforce PR review SLAs and pair reviewers to cut review time.
- Create a “pre‑prod” environment for parallel QA to eliminate serial wait times.
- Add feature flags for risky launches so bigger features can ship incrementally.
- Create a one‑page release checklist and automate parts of it (smoke tests).
- Triage and disable flaky tests that slow CI feedback.
- Reduce scope of next release to a minimum viable slice and ship it.

Stakeholder mapping — who to include and meeting agenda
- Who to map first: Engineering leads, QA/Test leads, DevOps/Platform, Design/UX, Release manager, Product partners (adjacent PMs), Data/Analytics, Security/Legal (if blocking releases), Customer Success (if release impacts customers).
- Quick 20–30 min meeting agenda
  - Purpose + context (2 min): “My top priority is cutting our time‑to‑market. I want to understand how we can move faster together.”
  - Their current priorities & biggest blockers to faster releases (8–10 min).
  - Specific suggestions they have and support they need (6–8 min).
  - Agree on 1–2 concrete actions and preferred communication cadence (2–4 min).
  - Ask who else to speak with and follow up commitments.

Meeting invite one‑liner
- “Intro + alignment — [Your name], new Senior Product Manager focusing on reducing time‑to‑market — 20 min to align on priorities and quick wins?”

Suggested comms to announce focus to your team (one‑line)
- “I’m focused on reducing our time‑to‑market this quarter — my priorities are removing release blockers, improving CI/Test reliability, and piloting feature flags. I’ll be running short working sessions — will share calendar invites.”

Measurement tips
- Start with a simple dashboard: lead time (idea→prod), change lead time (PR to deploy), release frequency, rollback rate, and defect escape rate.
- Use cohort comparisons (before vs. after pilot) and show small wins publicly.

30-day plan (Learn & Quick Wins)
Objectives
- Understand strategy, product, metrics, org structure, and top pain points.
- Build trust through targeted 1:1s and small, visible wins.

Actions (weeks 1–4)
- Schedule 1:1s (ideally first 2 weeks): manager, direct reports, PM peers, Eng lead, Design lead, Sales/CS, Marketing, Analytics, legal/compliance if applicable, and 3–5 key customers or power users.
- Read: strategy docs, roadmap, OKRs, top product specs, backlog, incident postmortems, key metrics dashboard for past 6–12 months.
- Observe demos and recent launches; get a feel for delivery cadence and QA.
- Do a quick product/UX audit: identify 3 low-effort/high-impact fixes (bug fixes, onboarding friction, copy changes) that you can push through in 2–3 sprints.
- Establish baseline metrics: activation, MAU/DAU, churn, conversion funnels, cycle time, NPS (or equivalent).
- Communicate: brief intro note to your team and key stakeholders stating your priorities for the first 30/60/90 days and openness to feedback.

Early-win project examples
- Backlog triage: remove/close stale tickets and highlight top 10 highest-impact items.
- Onboarding micro-improvement: redesign one screen or email to improve activation.
- Stakeholder clarifying deliverable: publish a one-page product health summary.

Success signals (30d)
- Completed 15–20 stakeholder 1:1s.
- Baseline metrics captured and shared.
- Delivered at least one visible improvement shipped within 30 days.
- Positive initial feedback from direct reports and key partners.

60-day plan (Align & Prototype)
Objectives
- Build a shared roadmap/priority framework and launch hypothesis-driven experiments.
- Formalize working norms and decision rights.

Actions (weeks 5–8)
- Synthesize findings from first 30 days into a “What I heard / What I recommend” memo and share with manager + leadership.
- Lead a cross-functional roadmap workshop to align on top priorities and trade-offs.
- Define prioritization criteria (customer value, revenue impact, confidence, effort) and apply to backlog.
- Implement or tighten product rituals: weekly roadmap sync, sprint review, monthly metrics review.
- Launch 1–2 small experiments/prototypes tied to highest-impact hypotheses (A/B test, pricing tweak, onboarding flow).
- Ensure analytics instrumentation is sufficient to measure experiments (event tracking, dashboards).
- Start talent/structure assessment: identify skills gaps and hiring/contractor needs.

Success signals (60d)
- Roadmap and prioritization framework agreed and published.
- Experiments launched with defined success metrics.
- Improvement in stakeholder clarity (survey or verbal feedback).
- Action plan for any resourcing/hiring needs.

90-day plan (Execute & Scale)
Objectives
- Deliver measurable results from experiments, operationalize processes, and present outcomes to execs.
- Establish cadence for sustained product delivery and team development.

Actions (weeks 9–12)
- Run experiments to completion; analyze and present results with recommendations (scale, iterate, or kill).
- Deliver at least one measurable feature/initiative that moves a key metric.
- Finalize 90–180 day roadmap aligned to company OKRs and resource plan.
- Document product processes (PRD template, intake process, decision matrix, design handoff).
- Set performance metrics and OKRs for the product org for the next quarter.
- Hold a 90-day review with manager and leadership: progress, wins, blockers, next priorities.
- Continue building team capability: 1:1 cadence, career plans, mentoring.

Success signals (90d)
- Measurable improvement in at least one key metric (e.g., activation +10%, feature adoption +X, cycle time -Y%).
- Roadmap and OKRs endorsed by execs.
- Clear processes and team alignment in place.

Stakeholder 1:1 agendas (quick templates)

  - Biggest risks/threats you see for the product/org.
  - Key stakeholders I should meet and political landmines.
  - Communication cadence you prefer.

  - What success looks like for you this quarter?
  - How do you prefer feedback and support?
  - Career goals / development areas.

- Peer (Tech/Design/Sales/CS) (30 minutes)

- Critical customer / power user (30 minutes)

Communication plan

- Weekly: concise product highlights (progress, decisions, blockers).
- Monthly: metrics dashboard + roadmap updates.
- 90-day: review presentation to leadership summarizing actions, results, roadmap.

Risks & mitigations
- Risk: moving too fast and alienating established team processes. Mitigation: ask before changing major processes; pilot changes.
- Risk: overcommitting to delivery vs. discovery. Mitigation: enforce time for discovery and experiments; protect focus time.
- Risk: misaligned expectations with execs. Mitigation: frequent check-ins and early validation of roadmap with stakeholders.

Context

What I heard (key themes)
- First-run experience is inconsistent: users hit confusing steps, unclear value, and multiple manual handoffs.  
- Instrumentation gaps: key onboarding events (progress points, drop-off reasons) are not fully tracked, so we lack clear funnels.  
- Product/design debt: several UX flows and copy issues create friction; a few bugs/perf issues further undermine trust.  
- Support load is rising: CS tickets spike around onboarding flows; common issues are repeatable and fixable.  
- Team constraints: PMs are stretched between triage and roadmap work; designers have high throughput demand; engineering capacity is limited.  
- Positives: core value is strong for engaged users; power users consistently cite X as a differentiator (insert specifics after interviews).

Evidence captured (actions you can fill/verify)

What I recommend (prioritized)
Immediate (0–30 days — deliverable: visible, low-risk wins)

4. Form an Onboarding Task Force (cross-functional; weekly): PMs, Design, Eng lead, CS, Analytics — charged with implementing fixes and running experiments.

Near term (31–60 days — align & test)
5. Run hypothesis-driven experiments (Owners: PM + Design + Analytics): A/B test a simplified onboarding flow and an in-product guidance variant. Define success metrics (activation lift, reduced support tickets).  
6. Strengthen CS handoff and in-product education: create templated flows, better contextual help, and a short guided tour for new users.  
7. Prioritization & resource decision: confirm whether onboarding work is top priority for next two sprint cycles (decision needed from execs).

Medium term (61–90 days — scale & measure)
8. If experiments validate changes, implement redesigned onboarding as a product initiative and track cohort improvements (D7 retention, conversion to key activation event).  
9. Process/ops: standardize PRD & intake for onboarding requests, reduce ad-hoc changes, and set an ongoing onboarding metric review cadence.

- Launch 2 experiments and validate at least one within 60 days.

Decisions needed from leadership
- Approve prioritization of onboarding work for the next 2 sprint cycles (yes/no).  
- Allocate engineering capacity: dedicated 20–40% capacity for the next 6 weeks for fixes + instrumentation.  
- Approve short-term budget for 1–2 temporary research/hiring needs (user sessions, contractor for analytics) if required.

Next steps (concrete)

- Week 1: Kick off rapid onboarding audit; schedule weekly Onboarding Task Force.  
- Week 1–2: Instrumentation sprint complete; baseline dashboards published.

- Eng leads: sprint capacity, bug fixes, instrumentation.  
- Analytics: event tracking, dashboards, experiment analysis.  
- CS: customer sessions, support ticket context and handoff improvements.

Closing
I’m recommending we treat onboarding as the top priority for the next 6 weeks so we can arrest activation decline and reduce churn. I’ll run the task force and provide weekly updates. Please let me know if you approve the resourcing ask and any changes to scope.

Thanks — I’ll incorporate feedback and send a calendar invite for the initial task force meeting.

Below are a focused, actionable 30–60–90 plan tailored to your new role (Senior Engineering Manager, 8-person team, start next Monday) with the explicit 3–6 month goal to cut release cycle time by 30% while boosting team morale — followed by a short announcement email you can send this week.

30–60–90 Day Plan

High-level objective: Reduce release cycle time by 30% while improving team morale and stability.

How I’m framing success (measurements to track)
- Cycle time (PR opened → production deploy) — primary metric; establish baseline in Week 1, target -30% by Day 90.
- Lead time, PR review time, deploy frequency.
- Change failure rate & mean time to recovery (MTTR).
- Team sentiment (pulse survey / eNPS) and qualitative feedback from 1:1s.

Days 0–30 (Observe, align, quick wins)
Objectives
- Build trust, gather facts, and set baseline metrics.
- Deliver 1–2 small, visible quick wins to show momentum.

Actions
- Day 1–10: Schedule 30–60 min one-on-ones with each direct report (listen: pain points, blockers, career goals).
- Run a short kickoff meeting (first week): share intent and invite input; set expectations for openness.
- Measure current state: collect metrics (cycle time, PR review time, deploy frequency, test flakiness). If metric tooling missing, instrument lightweight tracking (CSV + script).
- Do a value-stream walkthrough (pair with tech lead + SRE + QA + product): map steps from commit → prod; identify top 2–3 bottlenecks.
- Deliver quick wins (examples): reduce PR review backlog (triage + clear owner), automate a small manual step in pipeline, unblock a long-standing CI flake.
- Set meeting cadence: weekly team sync, bi-weekly ops/retro, 1:1s ongoing.

Owners: You (coordination), Tech Lead (technical diagnostics), SRE/CI owner, Product Manager (prioritization).

Success signals by Day 30
- Baseline metrics captured.
- 1–2 quick wins shipped and recognized.
- All 1:1s completed and a short summary of recurring themes created.

Days 31–60 (Experiment and improve)
Objectives
- Implement process and tooling changes to shorten cycle time.
- Continue morale actions and early coaching.

Actions
- Prioritize experiments from value-stream mapping (limit to 2–3 high-impact changes):
  - Reduce PR size policy + enforce quicker review SLAs (e.g., <24–48 hrs).
  - Improve CI pipeline: parallelize jobs, cache dependencies, remove redundant steps.
  - Introduce/expand feature flags and trunk-based practices for smaller deployable changes.
  - Increase automated test coverage in the slowest suites; quarantine flaky tests.
- Pilot a “fast-path” for low-risk changes to production (auto-merge rules + brief health checks).
- Establish a deployment playbook (rollforward/rollback, monitoring checks).
- Run a short internal learning session (pair-programming, postmortem blameless techniques).
- Start measuring impact of each experiment weekly; keep a visible dashboard.
- Continue recognition rituals (spotlight wins in team syncs; small rewards).

Owners: Tech Lead (code/practices), CI/SRE (pipeline), QA (tests), You (process, morale).

Success signals by Day 60
- One or two experiments showing measurable improvement in cycle time metrics (e.g., PR review time down, faster CI).
- Team feedback trending positive on changes.
- A tested playbook for safer, faster deployments.

Days 61–90 (Scale, standardize, sustain)
Objectives
- Lock in changes, scale successful experiments across the team, and embed continuous improvement.
- Aim to reach the 30% cycle-time reduction goal.

Actions
- Roll out successful pilots as standard processes across relevant repos.
- Automate recurring manual steps remaining in deployment flow.
- Formalize metrics dashboard and weekly review rituals; tie to team OKRs.
- Conduct a mid-term retro and a morale pulse survey; incorporate action items.
- Career conversations: establish development plans for each member based on 1:1 input.
- Celebrate milestones publicly and reinforce wins & learnings.
- Partner with product leadership to ensure backlog/prioritization supports smaller, incremental changes rather than large-batch releases.

Owners: You (OKRs, coaching), Tech Lead (standards), SRE/Platform (automation), Product (prioritization).

Success signals by Day 90
- Cycle time reduced near or at the -30% target (or clear trend with validated path to get there).
- Deploy process documented and reliable; fewer rollback incidents.
- Improved team sentiment and visible examples of career growth and recognition.

Risks & mitigations
- Risk: Too many changes at once → confusion. Mitigate: small experiments, clear communication, rollouts staged.
- Risk: Metrics inaccurate or noisy. Mitigate: validate instrumentation early and use multiple signals (qual + quant).
- Risk: Burning out team with process changes. Mitigate: prioritize workload, reduce nonessential meetings, include team in decisions.

Hi team,

I’m excited to share that I’ll be stepping in as Senior Engineering Manager for our team starting next Monday. Thank you for everything you’ve built so far — I’m proud of what we’ve achieved and eager to work with each of you.

Thanks — I’m excited to get started,
[Your name]

messages.content: It's been a tough few months pulling long hours and juggling projects, but it all paid off — I'm over the moon to say I was promoted to Senior Product Manager! I start May 15; my top goals are to shape the roadmap, win cross-functional alignment, and deliver an early high-impact win (my biggest worry is overcommitting and losing focus).
